# How to use this guide

Communicative English is a first-semester course of the INC 2021 B.Sc Nursing curriculum (2 credits, 40 hours of theory). It is about using English to do a nurse's work: listening to patients and colleagues, speaking on the ward and on the telephone, reading charts and orders, and writing notes, letters and reports.

**It is a college exam, not a university exam.** INC lists Communicative English among the courses examined by the college itself; the result is sent to the university for the mark sheet. The INC table gives 25 internal marks and 25 end-semester college exam marks (total 50); the college paper is usually set for 50 marks over 2 hours and then counted as 25. **The minimum pass for English is 40%** — lower than the 50% needed in other theory courses — but aim far higher, because this subject is easy to score in with practice.

**How the units are arranged.** One notes file for each of the seven INC units:

| Notes file | INC unit | Hours |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit 1 Communication and the roles of the four skills | I | 3 |
| Unit 2 Introduction to LSRGW: sounds, stress, intonation, vocabulary, tenses, linkers | II | 5 |
| Unit 3 Attentive listening | III | 5 |
| Unit 4 Speaking: conversation, telephone, handover, presentations | IV | 9 |
| Unit 5 Reading: strategies, abbreviations, visuals, reports, remedial grammar | V | 5 |
| Unit 6 Writing skills: history, notes, letters, reports, journals, abstract, CV | VI | 5 |
| Unit 7 LSRW in combination: critical thinking, instructions, error analysis | VII | 8 |

Language points named in the course competencies — paraphrasing, voice modulation, spelling, pause and silence — are covered in Unit 2.

## Exam pattern used for the mock paper

INC does not print a separate pattern for college exams, so the mock follows the 50-mark pattern of INC Appendix 3 with no internal choice. Your college may set it differently; confirm with your college.

| Part | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MCQ | 8 multiple-choice questions | 8 × 1 = 8 |
| Essay | 1 long answer (often a letter, report or situation) | 1 × 10 = 10 |
| Short | 4 short answers | 4 × 5 = 20 |
| Very short | 6 very short answers | 6 × 2 = 12 |
| **Total** | 2 hours | **50** |

Internal assessment (25 marks) comes from attendance, written assignments, presentations and two sessional exams. Many teachers also test speaking live (role play, handover, presentation), so practise aloud.

## Probability ratings

- **High** — asked in most papers in some form (letters, reports, SBAR handover, barriers to communication, tenses, active listening, telephone etiquette). Learn a full model answer.
- **Medium** — appears every few papers or inside a bigger question.
- **Low** — less common; useful for MCQs and 2-mark answers.

These are estimates from the syllabus hours and the usual style of first-year English papers in nursing colleges. They are not a promise of what will be asked.

## Where the marks usually come from

| Notes file | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Definition and process of communication, types, 7 Cs, barriers, nurse as listener/speaker/reader/writer |
| 2 | Types of listening, vowels and consonants, word stress, intonation, tenses, linkers, medical prefixes and suffixes |
| 3 | Active listening and SOLER, barriers to listening, verbatim reproducing and read-back, note-taking from lectures |
| 4 | Formal vs informal conversation, telephone conversation, SBAR handover, complaints, presentation skills, case presentation |
| 5 | Skimming and scanning, abbreviations (and dangerous ones), reading charts, parts of a prescription, idioms, spotting errors |
| 6 | Formal letters (leave, request, complaint), incident report, nurses' notes, anecdotal record, reflective journal, abstract, CV |
| 7 | Critical thinking, fact vs opinion, writing instructions, group discussion, error analysis |

## Scoring tips for this subject

1. **Format carries marks.** In letters, write every part: sender's address, date, receiver, subject, salutation, body in paragraphs, closing, signature and name. In reports, use headings. Examiners give marks for format even before reading the content.
2. **Use the situation given.** If the question names a ward, a patient or a date, use them. Invent sensible details (names, times) where none are given, but keep them realistic.
3. **Write in clear, correct, simple sentences.** One grammar mistake per line costs more than a short answer. Re-read every answer for tense, subject–verb agreement and spelling.
4. **For definitions, give definition + one example.** For 2-mark questions that is enough.
5. **Use tables for "differentiate"** (formal vs informal letter, hearing vs listening, skimming vs scanning, fact vs opinion).
6. **Learn the acronyms**: 7 Cs, SOLER, SBAR/ISBAR, SQ3R, SOAPIE, DAR, IMRaD, Gibbs' six stages, LSRW.
7. **Write model dialogues** in conversation questions — label speakers ("Nurse:", "Patient:") and show politeness phrases.
8. **Practise aloud.** Pronunciation, stress and intonation are learnt by speaking, not by reading. Record yourself on your phone and listen back.
9. **Keep a personal error log** (Unit 7) through the semester and revise it before the exam.

**Daily plan:** read one notes file, say its "Remember" list aloud, write one long and two short answers from the question bank without looking, then do the MCQs. In the last week, write one letter and one report every day and take the mock paper under time.

# Last-night revision sheet: Communicative English

## Unit 1 — Communication

- **Communication** = sending and receiving a message so both share the same meaning; **feedback** makes it two-way.
- Process: sender → encoding → message → channel → decoding → receiver → feedback; **noise** and **context** act throughout.
- Types: verbal (oral, written), non-verbal, visual; formal/informal; downward, upward, horizontal; intrapersonal, interpersonal, group, mass.
- **7 Cs**: clear, concise, concrete, correct, coherent, complete, courteous.
- Barriers: physical, physiological, language, psychological, cultural, organisational, personal.
- LSRW: listening and reading = receptive; speaking and writing = productive.
- Communicative competence: grammatical, sociolinguistic, discourse, strategic.

## Unit 2 — LSRGW basics

- Hearing (physical) vs listening (active). Listening types: discriminative, comprehensive, critical, empathetic, appreciative; faults: selective, passive.
- 44 English sounds: 24 consonants + 20 vowels (12 pure + 8 diphthongs). Schwa /ə/ is the commonest vowel. Watch /v/–/w/, /s/–/ʃ/, /θ/–/t/.
- Word stress: **PA**tient, **ME**dicine, hyper**TEN**sion, in**JEC**tion; noun **RE**cord / verb re**CORD**.
- Content words stressed, function words weak. Falling tone: statements and *wh*-questions; rising: yes/no questions.
- Voice modulation = pitch, volume, pace, tone, emphasis. Pause separates ideas; silence gives space.
- Medical words: prefix + root + suffix (brady-card-ia; gastr-ectomy).
- 12 tenses. Notes: past for actions done ("gave"), present for current state ("is drowsy"); "has vomited twice since morning".
- Linkers: addition (moreover), contrast (however), cause (because), result (therefore), sequence (first, then, finally).
- Paraphrase = same meaning, own words. British spelling: haemoglobin, oedema, paediatric, diarrhoea.

## Unit 3 — Attentive listening

- Process: receiving → understanding → remembering → evaluating → responding.
- **SOLER**: Sit squarely, Open posture, Lean, Eye contact, Relaxed.
- Tools: encouragers, open questions, clarifying, paraphrasing, reflecting feelings, summarising, silence. Avoid false reassurance and judging.
- Situations: announcement (who, what, where, when), description, narrative (sequence), instruction (verbs, numbers, warnings), discussion, demonstration.
- Listen for gist, specific information, detail, attitude, inference.
- **Verbatim**: verbal/telephone orders and critical results → write and **read back**; patient's words in quotation marks; say numbers digit by digit.
- Lectures: signposts, key words, Cornell / outline / mind map, review within a day.

## Unit 4 — Speaking

- Formal, neutral, informal situations; register. Factors: setting, topic, relationship, attitude, language.
- Polite request: "Could you…, please?" Permission: "May I…?" Disagree: "I see your point, but…"
- Complaint handling: listen, empathise, apologise, resolve, follow up.
- Telephone: identify self and area, purpose, read back, note message (date/time, caller, message, action, taken by), document.
- **SBAR**: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation (ISBAR adds Identify). Handover: changes, risks, pending tasks, questions.
- Rounds: name, diagnosis, events, findings, results, concerns, questions.
- Case presentation: identification → complaints → history → examination → investigations → management → nursing care → education → summary.
- Presentation: intro (topic, outline) → 3–5 points → conclusion and questions; signposts, eye contact, pauses.

## Unit 5 — Reading

- Skimming (main idea), scanning (one detail), intensive (orders), extensive (pleasure), critical (evaluate). **SQ3R**: survey, question, read, recite, review.
- Context clues: definition, example, contrast, word parts.
- Abbreviations: only approved ones. Avoid U, IU, QD, QOD, trailing zero (5.0), missing leading zero (.5).
- Visuals: title → labels/units → time scale → trend → highs/lows → meaning.
- Complete medicine order: patient, date/time, drug, dose, route, frequency, duration, instructions, signature. Unclear → ask.
- Reports: result, units, reference range, flags (H/L), trend; radiology: findings + impression.
- Grammar: a/an by sound (an hour, a university); suffering **from**; discuss (no "about"); cope **with**; each … **has**.

## Unit 6 — Writing

- Judged on task fulfilment, coherence and cohesion, vocabulary, grammar.
- Documentation: factual, accurate, complete, timely, organised, legible, signed, confidential; single-line correction, never erase.
- History: identification, chief complaints, present/past/family/personal/socio-economic history.
- Notes: narrative, **SOAPIE**, **DAR**.
- Summary: main ideas, own words, about one-third length, title.
- Anecdotal record: one incident, objective, date/time/place, separate comment, signatures.
- Formal letter: sender's address, date, receiver, **subject**, salutation, body (purpose–details–request), **Yours faithfully**, signature, name.
- Reflection — **Gibbs**: description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, action plan.
- Report: title, to/from/date, introduction, details, action, recommendations, signature; past tense, passive where suitable.
- Paper: narrow topic, literature, outline, own words + citation (no plagiarism), references. **Abstract**: IMRaD, 150–300 words, written last.
- CV: contact, objective, education, registration, experience, skills, training, achievements, references, declaration.

## Unit 7 — LSRW together

- Listen → read → think → speak → write → listen again.
- Critical thinking: source, evidence, fact vs opinion vs inference, bias, currency, verification; choose the safest evidence-based option.
- Instructions: title, things needed, numbered imperative steps, warnings, contact; **teach-back**.
- Group discussion: facts, listen, build on others, polite disagreement, stay on topic, summarise.
- Role play and demonstration with return demonstration.
- Error analysis: identify → cause → correct → error log. Types: grammatical, lexical, pronunciation, spelling, pragmatic, discourse.

## Exam checklist

- 50 marks, 2 hours: MCQ 8, essay 10, short 4 × 5, very short 6 × 2. Pass 40%.
- Letters and reports: full format first. Re-read every answer for tense, agreement and spelling.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: communication is the process of sending and receiving messages (ideas, information, feelings, instructions) between two or more people so that both reach a shared understanding. It is two-way, continuous, purposeful and depends on context.
2. Diagram: Sender → encoding → Message → Channel → decoding → Receiver → Feedback back to the sender; noise and context act at every stage.
3. Elements:
   - Sender: starts the message (staff nurse giving handover).
   - Encoding: putting the idea into words or signs.
   - Message: the content.
   - Channel: speech, telephone, chart, letter.
   - Decoding: receiver works out the meaning.
   - Receiver: the person meant to get it.
   - Feedback: response showing understanding (read-back of an order).
   - Noise: alarms, jargon, poor handwriting, fatigue.
   - Context: emergency, night shift, culture.
4. Types by means: verbal oral (handover, health talk), verbal written (nurses' notes, reports), non-verbal (touch, eye contact, posture, tone), visual (TPR chart, fall-risk sign).
5. Types by direction: downward (superintendent's circular), upward (reporting to the in-charge), horizontal (nurse to nurse).
6. Formal (ward rounds, reports) and informal (casual talk among colleagues).
7. By number of people: intrapersonal, interpersonal (nurse–patient), group (team meeting), mass (posters, radio).
8. Conclusion: in nursing, feedback is made deliberate (read-back, teach-back) because a misunderstood message can harm a patient.
questions.question: Define communication. Explain the process of communication with a diagram, and describe its types with examples from nursing practice.

questions.answer:
1. Barriers are anything that stops the receiver from getting the intended meaning.
2. Physical/environmental: noise, poor light, distance, masks → move closer, reduce noise, face the person.
3. Physiological: hearing loss, pain, sedation, fatigue → speak slowly and clearly, use writing or pictures, choose a comfortable time.
4. Language/semantic: different mother tongue, jargon, abbreviations → plain words, interpreter, check understanding.
5. Psychological: fear, anger, anxiety, grief → acknowledge feelings, listen first, stay calm.
6. Cultural: beliefs, gender norms, eye-contact customs → respect customs, ask preferences.
7. Organisational: rushed handover, unclear roles → standard formats such as SBAR, written records.
8. Personal: assumptions, interrupting, talking down → active listening, respect.
9. Teach-back: ask the patient to repeat the information in their own words.
10. 7 Cs: Clear (one idea, simple words), Concise (no extra words), Concrete (exact facts, times, amounts), Correct (facts, grammar, spelling), Coherent (logical order), Complete (all the receiver needs), Courteous (polite, respectful). Example: "Bed 6's pulse is 128 and irregular; please review" is clear, concrete and complete.
questions.question: What are the barriers to effective communication in a hospital? How can a nurse overcome them? Add a note on the 7 Cs of communication.

questions.answer:
- Listener: hears complaints and history, handover, doctors' and telephone orders; listens without interrupting; notices non-verbal cues; reads back critical information.
- Speaker: introduces self, explains procedures, gives health education in plain words, reports changes to doctors (SBAR), gives handover, calms relatives.
- Reader: reads case sheets, orders, reports, charts, labels, policies and books; never guesses an unclear order.
- Writer: writes nurses' notes, intake–output, care plans, reports, letters, discharge instructions; legibly, accurately, promptly — the record is a legal document.
- Listening and reading are receptive skills; speaking and writing are productive.
questions.question: Explain the communication roles of a nurse as a listener, speaker, reader and writer.

questions.answer:
- Definition: messages sent without words — facial expression, eye contact, posture, gestures, touch, distance, appearance, silence; paralanguage (tone, pitch, speed) shows how words are said.
- Importance: shows feelings more truthfully than words; when words and body language disagree, people believe the body language.
- Nurse observes patients' non-verbal cues — grimacing, restlessness, avoiding eye contact — as signs of pain, fear or depression.
- Nurse's own non-verbal behaviour (open posture, eye contact, gentle touch, calm tone) builds trust.
- Must respect culture: touch and eye contact rules differ; ask permission before touching.
questions.question: Describe non-verbal communication and its importance in nursing.

questions.answer:
- Medical records, consent forms, charts and reports are kept mostly in English.
- Textbooks, guidelines, journals and exams are in English.
- Teams from different states may share no regional language; English is the common language.
- Hospital software, equipment manuals and drug labels use English.
- Higher studies and jobs abroad need English.
- Patient safety: a misheard or misread word can cause a wrong patient, drug, site or time.
- The nurse also uses the patient's language and moves accurately between the two.
questions.question: Why is communicative English important for nurses in India?

questions.answer:
- Communicative competence: ability to use language correctly and also appropriately for the situation.
- Grammatical: correct words, grammar, pronunciation — "The patient has slept well."
- Sociolinguistic: suitable formality — "Good morning, Doctor" to a senior; first names with close friends.
- Discourse: connecting sentences into a logical whole — a handover that moves from situation to plan.
- Strategic: repairing breakdowns — "Sorry, could you repeat the time?" or using a picture.
questions.question: What is communicative competence? Describe its four components with examples.

questions.answer: Communication is the two-way process of sending and receiving messages — information, ideas or feelings — so that sender and receiver share the same meaning. Example: a nurse explains fasting before surgery and the patient repeats it back correctly.
questions.question: Define communication.

questions.answer: Feedback is the receiver's response that shows the sender how the message was understood. Example: after a telephone order, the nurse reads it back to the doctor to confirm.
questions.question: What is feedback in communication? Give an example.

questions.answer: Clear, concise, concrete, correct (also coherent, complete, courteous).
questions.question: List any four of the 7 Cs of communication.

questions.answer:
1. A tense shows the time of an action; three times (present, past, future) × four aspects (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous) = 12.
2. Simple present: The patient complains of headache (facts, current state).
3. Present continuous: The drip is running well (now).
4. Present perfect: She has vomited twice since morning (past linked to now).
5. Present perfect continuous: He has been coughing for three days.
6. Simple past: The doctor saw the patient at 10 am.
7. Past continuous: She was sleeping when I checked.
8. Past perfect: The fever had settled before the doctor came.
9. Past perfect continuous: He had been bleeding for an hour before admission.
10. Simple future: I will check the dressing at 2 pm.
11. Future continuous: We will be shifting her to the ward at noon.
12. Future perfect: The drip will have finished by 6 pm.
13. Future perfect continuous: By tomorrow he will have been fasting for 12 hours.
14. Rules for notes: simple past for actions done and observed ("gave", "ate"); present for the current state ("is drowsy"); simple past, not present perfect, with a stated past time ("I gave the injection at 8 am"); third-person -s ("the patient feels"); correct irregular forms (give–gave–given, bleed–bled–bled).
questions.question: What are tenses? Explain the twelve tenses of English with examples from nursing, and point out the tense rules nurses should follow in writing nurses' notes.

questions.answer:
1. English has 44 sounds in standard British pronunciation: 24 consonants and 20 vowels.
2. Consonants: air is stopped or narrowed — plosives /p b t d k g/, fricatives /f v θ ð s z ʃ ʒ h/, affricates /tʃ dʒ/ (chest, jaundice), nasals /m n ŋ/, lateral /l/, approximants /r w j/. Voiced (b, v, z) vs voiceless (p, f, s).
3. Vowels: air flows freely; 12 pure (short /ɪ e æ ʌ ɒ ʊ ə/, long /iː ɑː ɔː uː ɜː/) and 8 diphthongs (pain, eye, boil, dose, mouth, ear, care, pure). Schwa /ə/ is the commonest.
4. Word stress: one syllable louder and longer — PAtient, MEdicine, hyperTENsion, inJECtion; noun REcord vs verb reCORD.
5. Sentence stress: content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, negatives) stressed; function words weak. Contrastive stress changes meaning.
6. Intonation: falling for statements and wh-questions ("Where is the pain?"), rising for yes/no questions ("Are you comfortable?"), fall-rise for doubt, list intonation.
7. Indian learner errors: /v/–/w/ (vein, wound), /s/–/ʃ/ (sip, ship), /θ/ said as /t/, wrong stress (meDIcine), silent letters (pneumonia, psychology), syllable-timed rhythm.
8. Practice: dictionary stress marks, recording oneself, listening to good models.
questions.question: Explain the speaking component of LSRGW: consonants, vowels, word stress, sentence stress and intonation, with examples and common errors of Indian learners.

questions.answer:
- Discriminative: telling sounds apart — noticing a change in breath sounds or an alarm.
- Comprehensive (informational): understanding and remembering facts — handover, lecture.
- Critical (evaluative): judging truth or quality — weighing a health advertisement.
- Empathetic (therapeutic): understanding feelings — an anxious mother before her child's surgery.
- Appreciative: enjoyment — music.
- Faulty types: selective (only what interests us), passive (hearing without engaging).
- Active listening: full attention with responses and checking — the goal for nurses.
questions.question: Describe the different types of listening with clinical examples.

questions.answer:
- Linkers (connectives) join ideas and show how they relate; they make speech and writing coherent.
- Addition (and, moreover): The wound is clean; moreover, there is no swelling.
- Contrast (but, however, although): Although she slept, she still feels tired.
- Cause (because, since, due to): He was restless because of pain.
- Result (so, therefore): His pulse rose; therefore, I informed the doctor.
- Sequence (first, then, finally): First wash your hands, then put on gloves.
- Also example (for example), condition (if, unless), summary (in short).
questions.question: What are linkers? List linkers for addition, contrast, cause, result and sequence with one sentence each.

questions.answer:
- Most medical words are Greek/Latin parts: prefix (start) + root/combining form (main meaning) + suffix (end).
- brady- (slow) + cardi (heart) + -ia (condition) = bradycardia.
- tachypnoea = fast breathing; dysphagia = difficulty swallowing; hypoglycaemia = low blood sugar.
- gastritis = inflammation of stomach; appendicectomy = removal of appendix; hepatomegaly = enlarged liver; bronchoscopy = looking into the bronchi; colostomy = opening made in the colon; haematuria = blood in urine.
- Irregular plurals: diagnosis–diagnoses, bacterium–bacteria, vertebra–vertebrae.
- Use a medical dictionary for meaning, pronunciation and plural.
questions.question: Explain how medical words are built from prefixes, roots and suffixes. Give eight examples.

questions.answer:
- Voice modulation: changing pitch, volume, pace, tone and emphasis to suit message and listener.
- Low steady pitch sounds calm; volume enough to be heard, softer for private matters; slower pace for instructions, elderly and anxious patients and numbers; tone warm or urgent as needed; stress key words ("do NOT eat after midnight").
- Pause: short break that separates ideas, lets the listener absorb a number or instruction, and highlights what follows.
- Silence: deliberate quiet, with attentive body language, gives a distressed patient time to feel and continue; must not be cold or too long in formal talks.
questions.question: Write short notes on voice modulation, pause and silence in a nurse's speech.

questions.answer: A diphthong is a vowel sound that glides from one vowel to another within one syllable. Examples: /eɪ/ in 'pain', /aʊ/ in 'mouth' (also /əʊ/ in 'dose').

questions.answer: Paraphrasing is expressing someone's meaning in your own words without changing it. Example: 'nil by mouth after midnight' → 'please don't eat or drink anything after 12 tonight'.

questions.answer: PA-tient (first syllable); hy-per-TEN-sion (third syllable, the one before -sion).

questions.answer:
1. Definition: giving full attention to the speaker, understanding words and feelings, and showing understanding through responses.
2. Process: receiving → understanding → remembering → evaluating → responding.
3. Barriers: noise and interruptions, fatigue or worry, planning the reply, prejudging, selective listening, unfamiliar accent or words, information overload, distracting habits (phone).
4. Non-verbal technique SOLER: Sit squarely, Open posture, Lean slightly forward, Eye contact, Relaxed.
5. Verbal techniques: minimal encouragers ("Go on"), open questions ("How have you been sleeping?"), clarifying, paraphrasing, reflecting feelings ("You sound worried"), summarising, silence.
6. Avoid blocking responses: false reassurance, changing the subject, judging, early advice, blaming "why" questions.
7. Example: patient says her leg feels heavy; nurse sits, asks "Tell me more", paraphrases "your left leg is swollen and the calf hurts since morning — is that right?" and informs the doctor.
8. Benefits: accurate assessment, fewer errors, trust, calmer conflicts.
questions.question: What is attentive (active) listening? Describe the listening process, barriers to listening and the techniques a nurse uses to listen actively, with a short example.

questions.answer:
1. Announcements: short public messages — listen for who, what action, where, when (e.g. students to report to the Conference Hall, 2nd floor, at 2 pm).
2. Descriptions: features in order — size, shape, colour, position, use (a wound, a missing patient).
3. Narratives: events in time order — note sequence words and time expressions; draw a timeline (patient's history).
4. Instructions: action verbs, numbers, sequence words, warnings; repeat back before acting.
5. Discussions: topic, each speaker's view and reasons, agreement, decision.
6. Demonstrations: match each spoken step with the action; note rationale and safety points.
7. Purposes: gist, specific information, detail, attitude/opinion, inference.
8. Verbatim = word for word. Used for verbal/telephone orders (written and read back; signed later per policy), critical results (read back), patients' own statements (in quotation marks), names and numbers.
9. Example note: 11.30 pm — Patient says, "I can't breathe properly when I lie flat." Propped up; doctor informed.
10. Tips: write while listening, read numbers digit by digit (fifteen vs fifty).
questions.question: Explain listening in different situations — announcements, descriptions, narratives, instructions, discussions and demonstrations — and add a note on reproducing information verbatim in clinical practice.

questions.answer:
- S — Sit squarely facing the patient (or at a slight angle).
- O — Open posture: arms and legs uncrossed, showing openness.
- L — Lean slightly towards the person, showing interest.
- E — Eye contact that is comfortable and suited to culture, not staring.
- R — Relaxed manner, so the patient feels at ease.
- These non-verbal behaviours tell the patient the nurse is available and listening.
questions.question: Explain SOLER as a guide to attentive listening.

questions.answer:
- Verbatim means word for word, exactly as spoken or written.
- Verbal and telephone orders: written immediately and read back to the prescriber; signed later as per policy.
- Critical lab results given by phone: written and read back.
- Patient's own words about symptoms, refusal, threats or complaints: quoted in the notes, e.g. Patient says, "I don't want the operation."
- Names, hospital numbers, bed numbers and times.
- Statements during incidents or legal matters.
- Say numbers digit by digit to avoid confusing thirteen/thirty, fifteen/fifty.
questions.question: What is verbatim reproduction? When must a nurse reproduce information verbatim?

questions.answer:
- Before: read the topic, revise the last class, prepare the notebook with date and title.
- During: listen for signposts ("firstly", "another point", "to sum up"); write key words not every word; use abbreviations and symbols (↑, ↓, →, pt); mark points repeated or written on the board; note questions.
- Formats: outline (headings and sub-points), Cornell (cue column, notes column, summary), mind map.
- After: tidy the notes within a day, fill gaps from the textbook, write a five-line summary.
questions.question: How should a student listen to and take notes from a lecture?

questions.answer:
| Hearing | Listening |
| --- | --- |
| Physical — sound reaches the ear | Mental — attending, understanding, remembering, responding |
| Passive, automatic | Active, needs effort |
| No interpretation | Interprets words and feelings |
| Example: hearing a monitor beep | Noticing the rate on the monitor has changed |
- Barriers: noise, fatigue, prejudging the speaker, selective listening (also language difficulty, distractions).
questions.question: Differentiate hearing and listening. List four barriers to listening.

questions.answer: Listening for the overall main idea without attending to every detail — for example, knowing that a news item is about a dengue outbreak without noting every figure.

questions.answer: Short words or sounds that invite the speaker to go on: 'Mm-hm', 'I see', 'Go on', 'Yes…'.

questions.answer:
1. Handover: transfer of responsibility and information about a patient between nurses or teams — at shift change, transfer or for a procedure. Poor handover causes missed care, so a standard structure is used.
2. S — Situation: who you are, which patient, the problem now.
3. B — Background: diagnosis, admission date, relevant history, treatment so far.
4. A — Assessment: current vital signs and findings, your judgement.
5. R — Recommendation/Request: what you want done and by when.
6. ISBAR adds I — identify yourself and the patient.
7. Model: S: "Dr Rao, this is Staff Nurse Anu, Medical Ward 3, about Mr Prakash Singh, Bed 9 — his breathing has become fast in the last hour." B: "58 years, admitted two days ago with pneumonia, on IV antibiotics and oxygen by nasal prongs." A: "RR 30/min, SpO2 89% on oxygen, pulse 118, temperature 38.6 °C, BP 110/70; anxious and using neck muscles. I think his breathing is worsening." R: "Could you please come and see him now? Should I do anything before you arrive?"
8. Read back the orders, note the time, document the call.
9. Good handover: bedside where possible, structured, focuses on changes, risks and pending tasks, confidential, allows questions.
questions.question: What is handover (handoff)? Explain the SBAR technique and write a model SBAR telephone report to a doctor about a patient whose condition is getting worse.

questions.answer:
1. Telephone has no face or gestures, so clear voice, pace and structure matter.
2. Making a call: plan and keep chart and pen ready → greet and identify self and ward → confirm the right person → state the purpose briefly (SBAR) → note the reply and read back any order or result → close politely → document time, person, message and response.
3. Receiving a call: answer promptly — "Medical Ward 3, Staff Nurse Anu speaking. How can I help you?"; listen and note; confirm details; never give confidential information to an unidentified caller.
4. Clear speech: slow pace, spell names with a phonetic alphabet (A for Alpha), numbers digit by digit, no eating or side talk.
5. Courtesy: please, thank you, do not keep callers waiting without explanation.
6. Model message slip: Date/time 12 March 3.15 pm; For: Ward Sister, Surgical Ward; From: Mr Iqbal, Blood Bank, ext. 245; Message: two units for Bed 18 ready for collection; Action: send staff with requisition slip; Taken by: N. Joseph.
questions.question: Explain telephone conversation skills for nurses. Write the steps for making and receiving a call, and a model telephone message slip.

questions.answer:
- Formal: polite forms, titles, full sentences, no slang — viva, ward round, interview. "Would you mind checking the chart, Sister?"
- Neutral: polite but relaxed standard English — talking to patients, colleagues. "Could you check the chart, please?"
- Informal: short forms, first names, casual words — friends. "Can you look at the chart?"
- Factors: setting (ICU at night → quiet), topic (sensitive → private and gentle), social relationship (age, rank), attitude (respect, anxiety), language (shared language, vocabulary level). Also culture and the listener's health.
questions.question: Differentiate formal, informal and neutral conversation situations with examples. What factors influence the way we speak?

questions.answer:
- Steps: listen without interrupting → empathise → apologise for the experience → explain or resolve with a time frame → follow up and inform the in-charge.
- Model:
  Relative: "We've been waiting three hours for the report!"
  Nurse: "I can see you're upset, and I'm sorry you've had to wait so long."
  Relative: "Nobody tells us anything."
  Nurse: "I understand. I'll call the laboratory right now and come back to you within twenty minutes."
  Nurse (later): "The report is ready; the doctor will explain it at 4 pm."
- Keep a calm tone, no blame on others, and document if required.
questions.question: How should a nurse handle a complaint from a patient's relative? Write a short model dialogue.

questions.answer:
- Preparation: know purpose and audience; choose 3–5 main points; structure — introduction (greet, topic, outline), body, conclusion (summary, key message, questions); simple visuals with few words; rehearse and time.
- Delivery: stand straight, smile, eye contact around the room; clear voice with varied pitch and pauses; natural gestures; don't read slides.
- Signposts: "Today I'm going to talk about…", "Moving on to…", "To sum up…".
- Questions: listen, repeat, answer briefly; if unsure, promise to find out.
questions.question: List the steps of preparing and delivering a presentation.

questions.answer:
- An organised oral report about one patient presented to teachers and peers.
- Outline: introduction (initials, age, sex, ward, admission date, diagnosis) → chief complaints with duration → history (present, past, family, personal, social) → physical examination → investigations and results → medical/surgical management → nursing assessment, diagnoses, care plan, evaluation → health education and discharge plan → summary and questions.
- Language: past tense for history, present for current state; signposting; speak to the audience.
questions.question: What is a case presentation? Give its outline.

questions.answer: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation — a structured format for handover and reporting to doctors.

questions.answer: 'May I check your blood pressure?' and 'Is it all right if I open the window?' (also 'Do you mind if I sit here?').

questions.answer:
1. Skimming: fast reading for the main idea — headings, first lines (deciding if an article is useful).
2. Scanning: searching for one detail — an allergy, a result, an extension number.
3. Intensive reading: slow, careful, every word — orders, consent forms, exam questions.
4. Extensive reading: long texts for general understanding — novels, news; builds vocabulary.
5. Critical reading: question source, evidence, bias, fact vs opinion — health news.
6. SQ3R: Survey (headings, pictures), Question (turn headings into questions), Read (to answer them), Recite (answer without looking), Review (go over later).
7. Case sheet: check the right patient (name, hospital number) on every page, allergies, latest entries in date-time order, legibility and signatures; components: identification, history, progress notes, orders, medicine record, nurses' notes, charts, reports, consent, discharge summary.
8. Prescription of care: patient name, date and time, drug (generic name), dose and units, route, frequency, duration, special instructions, prescriber's signature; other orders (diet, activity, observations).
9. Rule: never guess an unclear order or abbreviation — clarify with the prescriber.
questions.question: Describe reading strategies with examples. Explain the SQ3R method and how a nurse should read a patient's case sheet and a doctor's prescription of care.

questions.answer:
1. Remedial grammar: revising and correcting grammar points that learners commonly get wrong.
2. Articles: 'a' before a consonant sound, 'an' before a vowel sound — a university, an hour, an MRI; 'the' for something specific or already mentioned; no article for general plurals/uncountables (Nurses work hard).
3. Prepositions: suffering from (not with), admitted to hospital on Monday at 6 pm, allergic to, cope with (not cope up with), discuss the plan (not discuss about), reply to, comply with.
4. Subject–verb agreement: Each of the patients has; The team is; Neither the nurse nor the doctors were (nearer subject); news is, scissors are; data show.
5. Corrections:
   - The patient have been vomiting → The patient has been vomiting.
   - She is suffering with diabetes since five years → She has been suffering from diabetes for five years.
   - I have given the injection yesterday → I gave the injection yesterday.
   - He is an unique case → He is a unique case.
   - Each patients need a name band → Each patient needs a name band.
6. Indian usages to avoid in formal writing: revert back, prepone, return back, 'I am having fever', 'Myself Anu', cousin brother.
questions.question: What is remedial grammar? Explain common errors in the use of articles, prepositions and subject–verb agreement, and correct five sentences commonly written by nursing students.

questions.answer:
- Abbreviations that are easily misread and have led to errors; many hospitals keep a do-not-use list.
- 'U' for units (read as 0 or 4) → write 'units'.
- 'IU' (read as IV or 10) → write 'international units'.
- 'QD', 'QOD' (daily and alternate days confused) → write 'daily', 'every other day'.
- Trailing zero (5.0 read as 50) → write 5. Missing leading zero (.5 read as 5) → write 0.5.
- Abbreviated drug names → write full name.
- OD can mean once a day or right eye — ambiguous; clarify.
- Use only the hospital's approved list; when in doubt, ask the prescriber.
questions.question: What are dangerous abbreviations? Why should nurses avoid them? Give examples.

questions.answer:
- Steps: read the title → labels and units on axes/columns → time scale → overall trend (rising, falling, steady, fluctuating) → highest and lowest values and anything outside normal → state the meaning and action.
- Tables: read across rows and down columns to the meeting cell.
- Flow sheets (vital-sign, intake–output, diabetic, neuro charts): read the latest entry and compare with earlier ones.
- Example: temperature 37 °C at 6 am rising to a peak of 39 °C at 2 pm, falling to 37 °C by 10 pm and steady overnight → fever spike in the afternoon, now settled; report and continue monitoring.
questions.question: How should a nurse read and interpret graphs, tables and flow sheets? Illustrate with a temperature chart.

questions.answer:
- Under the weather (slightly unwell): He is feeling under the weather today.
- On the mend (recovering): Her wound is on the mend.
- Keep an eye on (watch carefully): Keep an eye on the drip rate.
- Touch and go (uncertain, risky): It was touch and go during the night.
- In a nutshell (briefly): In a nutshell, the patient is stable.
- Also: break the ice, at the eleventh hour, burn the midnight oil.
- Idioms are for conversation, not for records or for patients who may not understand them.

questions.answer: The range of values found in healthy people for that test, printed beside the patient's result so that high (H) or low (L) results can be identified.

questions.answer:
Format and model:
To
The Nursing Superintendent,
District Hospital, (city)

Date: 20 March 2026

Subject: Request for replacement of two non-working suction machines in the Paediatric Ward

Respected Madam,

Paragraph 1 (purpose): I write to request two new suction machines for the Paediatric Ward. Two of our three machines have not worked since 15 March.

Paragraph 2 (details): The biomedical department examined them and reported that they cannot be repaired. We admit about 25 children daily, many with respiratory illness who need frequent suctioning. One machine is not enough, especially at night and in emergencies, and puts children at risk.

Paragraph 3 (request): I request that two machines be supplied at the earliest. The biomedical report is attached for your reference.

Thanking you,
Yours faithfully,
(Signature)
Name, Ward In-charge, Paediatric Ward

Marks points: sender/receiver details, date, clear subject, polite salutation, three clear paragraphs, reason with facts, specific request, closing 'Yours faithfully', signature with designation.

questions.answer:
1. Incident report: a factual, objective written record of an unexpected event that harmed or could have harmed a patient, staff or visitor; used to take action and prevent recurrence. Written promptly; no blame or opinion.
2. Model:
   Incident report
   Patient: Mr K. Nair, 76 years, Bed 21, Male Medical Ward, Hosp. No. 30718
   Date/time of incident: 9 April, 3.10 am
   Description: Patient found sitting on the floor beside the bed. He said, "I wanted to go to the toilet and my legs gave way." Side rails were down; call bell out of reach.
   Assessment: Conscious, oriented, pain in right hip, no bleeding. T 36.8 °C, P 92/min, R 20/min, BP 140/90 mmHg.
   Action taken: Lifted back to bed by two staff; duty doctor informed at 3.15 am and examined at 3.25 am; X-ray of right hip ordered; side rails raised, call bell and urinal within reach; family informed at 7 am.
   Recommendations: fall-risk assessment on admission for elderly patients; night-time toileting rounds.
   Reported by: name, designation, date and time.
3. Language: past tense, patient's words in quotation marks, exact times, no guessing or blame.
questions.question: What is an incident report? Write an incident report on an elderly patient who fell from bed during the night.

questions.answer:
- Factual: what is seen, heard, measured, done; no labels or guesses.
- Accurate: exact values, times, spelling; approved abbreviations only.
- Complete: care, responses, communication with others.
- Timely: written soon after care, never before.
- Organised in date-time order; legible in ink or the electronic system; signed with name and designation; confidential.
- Correction: draw a single line through the error so it remains readable, write 'error', initial and date it, then write the correct entry. No correction fluid, overwriting, tearing pages or blank lines.
- "Not written = not done" — the record is a legal document.
questions.question: State the principles of good documentation and the correct way to correct an error in nursing records.

questions.answer:
- A short, factual written description of one specific incident of behaviour, written soon after observation, with the observer's comment kept separate.
- Features: one incident per record; objective description; date, time, place; interpretation separate; signed by observer and student.
- Model: Student: Ms R. Thomas, 1st year; Area: Female Medical Ward; 18/03, 10.15 am. Incident: while giving a bed bath to an elderly patient, she drew the curtains, explained each step, kept unexposed parts covered and added a blanket when the patient felt cold. Comment: respects privacy and responds to needs. Recommendation: share practice with peers. Signatures.
questions.question: What is an anecdotal record? Write its features and a model.

questions.answer:
- A written reflection on a learning experience that links theory and practice and helps professional growth.
- Gibbs' cycle: Description (what happened) → Feelings → Evaluation (good and bad) → Analysis (make sense, link to theory) → Conclusion (what else could be done) → Action plan (what next time).
- Example: first BP check without help; hands shook (description); felt nervous with the son watching (feelings); patient thanked me (evaluation); I focused on being judged rather than explaining (analysis); explaining first would relax us both (conclusion); next time explain each step aloud and practise more (action plan).
- First person, past tense, confidentiality.
questions.question: What is a reflective journal? Explain Gibbs' reflective cycle with a short example.

questions.answer:
- An abstract is a short complete summary (usually 150–300 words, as per limit) at the start of a paper so readers can judge its relevance.
- Structured (IMRaD): Background/Introduction (problem and aim), Methods (design, setting, sample, tools), Results (main findings), Conclusion/Discussion (meaning and recommendation), Keywords (3–5).
- Written last; past tense for methods and results; no references; abbreviations explained.
questions.question: What is an abstract? Describe the structure of a structured abstract.

questions.answer:
- Read the whole text to understand it.
- Underline the main idea of each paragraph.
- Omit examples, repetition and minor details.
- Write the main ideas in your own words, linked logically.
- Keep to about one-third of the original length.
- Check meaning is unchanged and nothing important is missing; add a title.
- Qualities: brief, accurate, complete for main ideas, objective, own words, coherent.
questions.question: Write a summary of a passage: steps and qualities of a good summary.

questions.answer: Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan, Intervention, Evaluation — a format for writing nurses' notes.
questions.question: Expand SOAPIE.

questions.answer: 'Yours faithfully' when the receiver is addressed as 'Dear Sir/Madam' (name not known); 'Yours sincerely' when the receiver is addressed by name.

questions.answer: Contact details, career objective, education, nursing council registration, clinical experience, skills, training/certificates, achievements and activities, references, declaration.
questions.question: List the main headings of a resume for a fresh nursing graduate.

questions.answer:
1. Critical thinking: careful, purposeful thinking that questions information, examines evidence and reaches reasoned judgements instead of accepting things at face value.
2. Questions to ask: Who is the source and are they reliable? What is the main claim? What evidence supports it? Is it fact or opinion? Is anything biased, missing or exaggerated? Is it current? Does it match other trusted sources? What should I do?
3. Fact (can be checked: temperature 38.5 °C), opinion (belief: 'best hospital'), inference (conclusion from facts: high temperature and chills suggest infection).
4. Signal words of opinion: best, should, I believe, clearly, everyone knows.
5. Evaluating options: list options, advantages, disadvantages and risk; choose the safest evidence-based, policy-compliant option; explain it clearly.
6. Example: relative asks to give a home herbal remedy → explain politely that only prescribed medicines are given and inform the doctor.
7. Practice: weighing health news and forwarded messages, checking orders, interpreting charts, deciding priorities, reporting with evidence.
questions.question: What is critical thinking? Explain critical thinking strategies for listening and reading, and how a nurse uses them in practice.

questions.answer:
1. Error analysis: identifying errors, finding their cause and correcting them systematically.
2. Listening: missed numbers, misheard names → distraction, accent → note while listening, read back, ask for repetition.
3. Speaking: wrong stress, /v/–/w/, mother-tongue patterns, fast flat speech → first-language influence, nervousness → listen to models, record self, slow down, pause.
4. Reading: misreading words/numbers, guessing abbreviations → haste, poor handwriting → read twice, clarify, dictionary.
5. Writing: tense, agreement, prepositions, spelling, run-ons, missing time and signature → translation, hurry → plan, re-read, error log, standard formats.
6. Types: grammatical, lexical, pronunciation, spelling, pragmatic (wrong for the situation), discourse (wrong order).
7. Faulty note: "Patient is complaining of severe headache since morning, he is vomited two times. Doctor was informed and he told to give medicine. Patient now feel better."
8. Corrected: "11.00 am — Patient has been complaining of severe headache since 7 am. He has vomited twice. Dr Gupta informed at 10.15 am; medicine given as ordered (see medicine chart). At 11.00 am patient says the headache is better, 3/10. — Signature, name, designation."
9. Keep a personal error log and review weekly.
questions.question: What is error analysis? Describe common errors in listening, speaking, reading and writing with their causes and correction strategies. Correct a faulty nurses' note.

questions.answer:
- Rules: clear title; list of things needed; numbered steps in order; each begins with an action verb; one action per step; warnings separate and highlighted; plain words, pictures if useful; what to do if there is a problem and whom to contact.
- Model — How to care for your wound at home: 1. Wash hands before touching the dressing area. 2. Keep the dressing clean and dry. 3. Do not soak the wound until the doctor says it has healed. 4. Look at it every day. 5. Come to the dressing clinic on the date on your card. Contact the hospital at once if it becomes red, swollen, very painful, smelly, leaks pus or you get a fever.
- Check understanding with teach-back.
questions.question: How should a nurse write instructions for a patient? Write model home-care instructions.

questions.answer:
- A structured conversation in which a group shares views on a topic to reach understanding or a decision; assesses knowledge, clarity, reasoning, listening, leadership and teamwork.
- Do's: start if you have a clear point; support with facts and examples; listen and build on others; disagree politely ("I see it differently because…"); bring the group back to the topic; summarise if asked.
- Don'ts: shout, interrupt, dominate, make personal remarks, remain silent throughout, go off-topic.
questions.question: What is a group discussion? List the do's and don'ts for participants.

questions.answer:
- Spoken presentation of information or findings to listeners — handover, rounds, staff meeting, class.
- Structure: opening (topic and purpose) → main body (facts in order: time, priority or SBAR) → closing (conclusion, recommendation, questions).
- Qualities: brief, accurate, organised, clear voice, numbers said slowly.
- Model: "This is the infection-control report for March. 42 admissions; two catheter-related urinary infections, both with catheters in place over five days. I recommend a daily check of whether each catheter is still needed. Any questions?"
questions.question: What is an oral report? Give its structure and a short model.

questions.answer:
- Listen: to the patient's and family's history; note exact words and key facts.
- Read: referral letter, earlier reports, admission orders.
- Think: identify priorities and risks.
- Speak: welcome and orient the patient, explain routine, report findings to the doctor (SBAR).
- Write: admission assessment, nurses' notes, care plan.
- Listen again: to feedback and new orders; read back.

# Unit 1: Communication and the roles of listeners, speakers, readers and writers

This unit covers INC Unit I (3 hours). It explains what communication is, how it works, what can go wrong, and why a nurse needs good English for each of the four skills: listening, speaking, reading and writing (LSRW).

## 1.1 What is communication?

**Communication** is the process of sending and receiving messages — ideas, information, feelings and instructions — between two or more people so that both reach a shared understanding.

The word comes from the Latin *communis*, meaning "common". Communication has worked only when the meaning in the receiver's mind is the same as the meaning the sender intended. Speaking or writing alone is not communication; the message must be understood.

Key points in the definition:

- It is a **two-way process** — there is always a sender and a receiver, and the roles keep changing.
- It is **continuous** — even silence, a frown or a delay sends a message.
- It is **purposeful** — to inform, to instruct, to persuade, to comfort or to build a relationship.
- It is **contextual** — the place, time, culture and relationship change how a message is understood.

**Communicative English** means English used to get things done with other people: to ask, explain, report, reassure, complain, agree or record. The focus is on clear, correct and suitable language rather than on literature.

## 1.2 The process of communication

```text
  SENDER --> encodes --> MESSAGE --> CHANNEL --> decodes --> RECEIVER
    ^          (words, gestures)   (speech, chart,             |
    |                               phone, letter)             |
    |                                                          |
    +---------------------- FEEDBACK <-------------------------+

           NOISE (anything that disturbs the message) acts at every stage
           CONTEXT (setting, culture, relationship) surrounds the whole process
```

| Element | Meaning | Ward example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sender (source) | The person who starts the message | The staff nurse giving a handover |
| Encoding | Turning an idea into words, signs or symbols | Choosing clear words: "Bed 4 needs a fresh dressing at 2 pm" |
| Message | The content — facts, feelings, orders | The patient's condition and plan |
| Channel (medium) | The route the message travels by | Face-to-face talk, telephone, case sheet, text message |
| Decoding | The receiver working out the meaning | The incoming nurse understanding "fresh dressing at 2 pm" |
| Receiver | The person for whom the message is meant | The nurse coming on duty |
| Feedback | The receiver's response that shows how the message was understood | "So the dressing is due at 2 pm — I'll do it." |
| Noise | Anything that distorts the message | Monitor alarms, poor handwriting, jargon, fatigue |
| Context | The surrounding situation | An emergency, a night shift, a crowded OPD |

**Feedback** is what makes communication two-way. Without it the sender cannot know whether the message was received correctly. In clinical work feedback is made deliberate: the receiver **reads back** or **repeats** important information (closed-loop communication).

## 1.3 Types of communication

### By the means used

| Type | Description | Nursing examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Verbal – oral | Spoken words | Handover, explaining a procedure, telephone call |
| Verbal – written | Written or typed words | Nurses' notes, incident report, discharge instructions |
| Non-verbal | Messages without words: face, eyes, posture, gestures, touch, distance, tone, silence | A reassuring touch, eye contact, sitting at the bedside |
| Visual | Charts, graphs, signs, pictures, colours | TPR chart, fall-risk sign above a bed, pictorial pain scale |

Non-verbal signs often carry more emotion than words. If words and body language disagree ("I'm fine" with a grimace), people usually believe the body language, so a nurse must observe both.

**Paralanguage** is *how* something is said — tone, pitch, loudness, speed, pauses. "Take your medicine" can sound kind or rude depending on paralanguage alone.

### By formality and direction

- **Formal** — follows official lines and set formats: duty rosters, circulars, reports, ward rounds.
- **Informal** — casual talk between colleagues; quick, but can spread rumours ("grapevine").
- **Downward** — from senior to junior: the nursing superintendent's instructions.
- **Upward** — from junior to senior: reporting a change in a patient to the ward in-charge or doctor.
- **Horizontal (lateral)** — between people of the same level: nurse to nurse, unit to unit.

### By the number of people

- **Intrapersonal** — talking to oneself, thinking, reflecting.
- **Interpersonal** — between two people, for example nurse and patient.
- **Group** — a team meeting or a health talk to a small group.
- **Mass / public** — a talk to a large audience, posters, radio.

## 1.4 Principles of effective communication: the 7 Cs

| C | Meaning | Weak | Better |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Clear | One idea at a time, simple words | "Patient not OK, check" | "Bed 6's pulse is 128 and irregular; please review" |
| Concise | No unnecessary words | "I would like to inform you that it seems the patient may have…" | "The patient has vomited twice" |
| Concrete | Specific facts, figures, times | "Drank a lot" | "Drank 1,200 ml since 8 am" |
| Correct | Right facts, right grammar, right spelling | "Patient is hypertention" | "The patient has hypertension" |
| Coherent | Ideas follow a logical order | Jumping between topics | Situation → background → assessment → request |
| Complete | Everything the receiver needs | Missing the patient's name or bed | Name, bed, problem, action needed |
| Courteous | Polite and respectful | "Sit there and wait" | "Please have a seat; I'll call you in a few minutes" |

Some books add **Considerate** (thinking of the receiver's needs) instead of one of the above; the idea is the same.

## 1.5 Barriers to communication

| Barrier | Examples in hospital | How a nurse overcomes it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Physical / environmental | Noise, poor light, distance, a mask, a closed door | Move closer, reduce noise, face the person |
| Physiological | Hearing loss, pain, fatigue, sedation, speech defect | Speak slowly and clearly, use writing or pictures, wait for comfort |
| Language and semantic | Different mother tongue, jargon, abbreviations, words with two meanings | Use simple words, avoid jargon, use an interpreter, check understanding |
| Psychological / emotional | Fear, anxiety, anger, grief, prejudice | Acknowledge feelings, listen first, be calm |
| Cultural | Different beliefs about illness, gender rules, eye contact norms | Respect customs, ask preferences, involve family appropriately |
| Organisational | Too many levels, unclear roles, rushed handovers | Use standard formats (SBAR), written records |
| Personal | Poor listening, assumptions, interrupting, talking down | Practise active listening and respect |

A useful habit: after giving important information, ask the patient to **say it back in their own words** (the teach-back method). This checks understanding without making the patient feel tested.

## 1.6 Why English matters for a nurse in India

- **Medical records** — case sheets, nurses' notes, medicine charts, consent forms and reports are mostly kept in English.
- **Education** — textbooks, journals, guidelines and examinations are in English.
- **Team work** — doctors, nurses and technicians from different states may share no regional language; English becomes the common one.
- **Technology** — hospital information systems, equipment manuals and drug labels use English.
- **Career** — higher studies, nursing jobs abroad and international examinations test English.
- **Patient safety** — a misheard or misread word (a wrong name, wrong side, wrong time) can harm a patient. Many errors in hospitals are communication errors.

A nurse also needs the **patient's language**. Good communicative English does not replace the local language; it lets the nurse move accurately between the record (English) and the patient (often a regional language).

## 1.7 Communication roles of listeners, speakers, readers and writers as healthcare professionals

The four skills are grouped as **receptive** (listening, reading — taking in) and **productive** (speaking, writing — giving out). They are also grouped as **oral** (listening, speaking) and **written** (reading, writing).

```text
                 RECEPTIVE          PRODUCTIVE
   ORAL          Listening          Speaking
   WRITTEN       Reading            Writing
```

### The nurse as a listener

- Listens to the patient's complaints, worries and history — often the first clue to a problem.
- Listens to handover, doctors' instructions, telephone orders and announcements.
- Listens with attention, without interrupting, and checks meaning ("Do you mean the pain started after food?").
- Listens to non-verbal cues — sighs, silence, a shaky voice.
- Repeats critical information back to confirm it.

### The nurse as a speaker

- Greets, introduces self and explains procedures before doing them.
- Gives health education in simple words the patient can follow.
- Reports changes in a patient's condition to doctors and seniors clearly and quickly.
- Gives handover at the end of a shift and speaks during rounds and case presentations.
- Speaks politely to relatives, calms anxious people and handles complaints.
- Uses a suitable tone, speed, volume and level of language for each listener.

### The nurse as a reader

- Reads case sheets, doctors' orders, prescriptions of care, lab reports and previous nurses' notes.
- Reads charts, flow sheets, graphs and tables (TPR, intake–output, partograph).
- Reads hospital policies, circulars, equipment manuals and medicine labels.
- Reads textbooks, journals and news to keep knowledge up to date.
- Reads carefully and asks when something is unclear — never guesses at an unclear order.

### The nurse as a writer

- Writes nurses' notes, observations, intake–output and care plans.
- Writes handover notes, incident reports, requisitions and letters.
- Writes patient education leaflets and discharge instructions in plain language.
- Writes assignments, reflective journals, projects and research abstracts as a student.
- Writes legibly, accurately and promptly; a record is a legal document ("not written = not done").

## 1.8 Communicative competence and LSRW strategies

**Communicative competence** is the ability to use language not just correctly but **appropriately** for the situation. It has four parts:

| Part | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grammatical (linguistic) | Correct words, grammar, pronunciation | "The patient has slept well" (not "has sleeped") |
| Sociolinguistic | Right level of formality for the person and place | "Good morning, sir" to a senior doctor; first name with a close colleague |
| Discourse | Linking sentences into a connected whole | A handover that flows from situation to plan |
| Strategic | Repairing a breakdown in communication | "Sorry, could you repeat the last dose time?" or drawing a picture |

**Communicative strategies** for each skill:

| Skill | Useful strategies |
| --- | --- |
| Listening | Predict the topic, listen for key words, note numbers and names, ask for repetition, read back |
| Speaking | Plan the main point, use short sentences, check the listener's understanding, use examples |
| Reading | Skim for the main idea, scan for a detail, guess words from context, check abbreviations |
| Writing | Plan, write, then revise; use headings and lists; keep to facts; check spelling and grammar |

## 1.9 Therapeutic and social communication (a preview)

- **Social communication** — everyday conversation between equals for friendship or business.
- **Therapeutic communication** — purposeful, patient-centred communication that helps the patient express feelings, understand care and cope. The nurse listens more than she speaks, uses open questions, reflects feelings, and keeps the focus on the patient.

This idea is studied in detail in Nursing Foundations and Psychology; in English you practise the **language** for it (open questions, reflecting, summarising — see Units 3 and 4).

## Remember

- Communication = sending and receiving a message with **shared understanding**; feedback makes it two-way.
- Elements: sender, encoding, message, channel, decoding, receiver, feedback, noise, context.
- Types: verbal (oral, written), non-verbal, visual; formal/informal; upward, downward, horizontal.
- 7 Cs: clear, concise, concrete, correct, coherent, complete, courteous.
- Barriers: physical, physiological, language, psychological, cultural, organisational, personal.
- LSRW: listening and reading are receptive; speaking and writing are productive.
- Nurses are listeners, speakers, readers and writers every shift — and every record is a legal document.
- Communicative competence = grammatical + sociolinguistic + discourse + strategic.
