# Unit 2: Introduction to LSRGW — listening, speaking sounds, medical vocabulary, grammar and simple writing

This unit covers INC Unit II (5 hours). LSRGW stands for **L**istening, **S**peaking, **R**eading, **G**rammar and **W**riting. It also covers the language points named in the course competencies: pronunciation, vocabulary, grammar, paraphrasing, voice modulation, spelling, pause and silence.

## 2.1 L — Listening: different types of listening

**Hearing** is the physical act of sound reaching the ear. **Listening** is the active mental process of attending to, understanding, remembering and responding to what is heard. A nurse may hear a monitor all night without listening to it; she listens when she notices the rate has changed.

| Type of listening | Purpose | Clinical example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Discriminative | Telling sounds apart | Noticing a change in a patient's breathing sound or a different alarm tone |
| Comprehensive (informational) | Understanding and remembering facts | Listening to a lecture or a handover |
| Critical (evaluative) | Judging whether a message is sound or true | Deciding if a medicine advertisement makes believable claims |
| Empathetic (therapeutic) | Understanding feelings from the speaker's point of view | Listening to a mother anxious about her baby's surgery |
| Appreciative | Enjoying | Listening to music or a good speech |
| Selective | Hearing only what interests us (a fault) | Catching the time of the next class but missing the room change |
| Passive | Hearing without responding or engaging | Half-listening while writing notes |
| Active | Full attention, with verbal and non-verbal responses and checking | Nodding, paraphrasing and asking a question in a patient interview |

Practice material for this unit: news bulletins, hospital announcements, telephone conversations and instructions. While listening, note **who, what, where, when, how much** and any **number**.

## 2.2 S — Speaking: the sounds of English

English spelling and English sounds do not match one-to-one. "Cough", "though", "through" and "rough" all end in *-ough* but sound different. So we learn **sounds (phonemes)**, written in phonetic symbols between slashes, for example /p/.

Standard British English (Received Pronunciation, the model used in most Indian textbooks) has **44 sounds: 24 consonants and 20 vowels (12 pure vowels and 8 diphthongs).**

### Consonants

A **consonant** is a sound made when the air is stopped or narrowed somewhere in the mouth or throat.

| Group | Sounds | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plosives (stops) — air stopped then released | /p/ /b/ /t/ /d/ /k/ /g/ | pain, blood, temperature, dose, cough, gauze |
| Fricatives — air squeezed through a narrow gap | /f/ /v/ /θ/ /ð/ /s/ /z/ /ʃ/ /ʒ/ /h/ | fever, vein, thermometer, the, swab, zinc, shock, measure, heart |
| Affricates — stop + friction | /tʃ/ /dʒ/ | chest, jaundice |
| Nasals — air through the nose | /m/ /n/ /ŋ/ | mouth, nurse, lung |
| Lateral | /l/ | liver |
| Approximants (semi-vowels) | /r/ /w/ /j/ | rest, ward, yellow |

**Voiced** consonants make the vocal cords vibrate (/b/, /d/, /v/, /z/); **voiceless** ones do not (/p/, /t/, /f/, /s/). Put your fingers on your throat while saying "vvv" and "fff" to feel the difference.

Common Indian learner difficulties and fixes:

- **/v/ and /w/** — "vein" (top teeth on lower lip) vs "wound" (rounded lips, no teeth).
- **/s/ and /ʃ/** — "sip" vs "ship"; "sore" vs "shore". Saying "sugar" correctly needs /ʃ/.
- **/z/** — "zinc", "dose" (/s/) vs "doze" (/z/).
- **/θ/ and /ð/** — "thermometer", "three" (tongue between the teeth, no voice); "the", "this" (with voice). Avoid replacing them with /t/ or /d/.
- **Silent letters** — psychology, pneumonia, psoriasis (silent p); knee, knife (silent k); haemorrhage, rhythm (silent h after r); mortgage (silent t); honest (silent h).

### Vowels

A **vowel** is a sound made with the air flowing freely through the mouth; the tongue and lips shape it.

- **Short pure vowels**: /ɪ/ (bit), /e/ (bed), /æ/ (cat), /ʌ/ (cup), /ɒ/ (hot), /ʊ/ (put), /ə/ (the first sound of "about" — called **schwa**).
- **Long pure vowels**: /iː/ (feed), /ɑː/ (heart), /ɔː/ (ward), /uː/ (food), /ɜː/ (nurse).
- **Diphthongs** (a glide from one vowel to another): /eɪ/ (pain), /aɪ/ (eye), /ɔɪ/ (boil), /əʊ/ (dose), /aʊ/ (mouth), /ɪə/ (ear), /eə/ (care), /ʊə/ (pure).

Length changes meaning: "ship" /ɪ/ vs "sheep" /iː/; "full" /ʊ/ vs "fool" /uː/. The **schwa** is the most common sound in English because most unstressed syllables use it: a**bout**, nur**ses**, **hos**pit**al**.

## 2.3 Word stress

In every English word of two or more syllables, one syllable is said **louder, longer and higher** — the stressed syllable. Wrong stress can make a correct word hard to understand.

| Word | Stressed syllable | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **HOS**-pi-tal | 1st | |
| **PA**-tient | 1st | Not "pa-TIENT" |
| **ME**-di-cine | 1st | A common Indian slip is "me-DI-cine" |
| **TEM**-pe-ra-ture | 1st | |
| di-ag-**NO**-sis | 3rd | |
| hy-per-**TEN**-sion | 3rd | Words ending in *-sion*, *-tion* stress the syllable before |
| in-**JEC**-tion | 2nd | Same *-tion* rule |
| a-**NA**-ly-sis / a-na-**LY**-ti-cal | moves | Stress can move when the word changes form |
| **PRE**-sent (noun) / pre-**SENT** (verb) | 1st / 2nd | Also **RE**-cord / re-**CORD**, **IN**-crease / in-**CREASE** |

Simple rules (with exceptions):

1. Most two-syllable nouns and adjectives stress the first syllable: **NUR**ses, **DOC**tor, **HAP**py.
2. Most two-syllable verbs stress the second: re**PORT**, ad**MIT**, ex**PLAIN**.
3. Words ending in *-tion, -sion, -ic, -ical, -ity, -ian* stress the syllable just before the ending: in-**FEC**-tion, pae-di-**A**-tric, ac-**TI**-vi-ty, phy-**SI**-cian.
4. A dictionary marks stress with ˈ before the stressed syllable: /ˈtemprətʃə/.

## 2.4 Sentence stress and rhythm

In a sentence, **content words** carry stress; **function words** are usually weak and quick.

- Content words: nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs, question words, negatives (not, never).
- Function words: articles (a, the), prepositions (in, at), auxiliaries (is, have, can), pronouns, conjunctions.

Example: "The **PAtient** in **BED FOUR** has a **HIGH FEver**."

Moving the stress changes the meaning (contrastive stress):

- "**I** gave the medicine at 8." (not someone else)
- "I gave the medicine at **8**." (not at 9)

English is **stress-timed**: stressed syllables come at roughly regular intervals and the weak ones are squeezed between them. Many Indian languages are syllable-timed (every syllable gets equal time), which is why Indian English can sound fast or flat to outsiders. Weakening the function words makes speech clearer, not less clear.

## 2.5 Intonation

**Intonation** is the rise and fall of the voice (pitch) across a sentence. It shows the type of sentence and the speaker's attitude.

| Pattern | Used for | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Falling ↘ | Statements, commands, *wh*-questions (what, where, when) | "Your test is at ten. ↘" "Where is the pain? ↘" |
| Rising ↗ | Yes/no questions, checking, showing interest | "Are you comfortable? ↗" "Did you sleep? ↗" |
| Fall-rise ↘↗ | Doubt, politeness, something left unsaid | "It's not too bad… ↘↗ (but I'm worried)" |
| Rise-fall ↗↘ | Strong feeling, surprise | "Really! ↗↘" |
| List intonation | Rise on each item, fall on the last | "Bring the gauze ↗, the tape ↗ and the scissors ↘." |

A flat or falling tone on "Can I help you?" can sound bored or rude; a gentle rise sounds caring.

## 2.6 Voice modulation, pause and silence

**Voice modulation** is changing the voice to suit the message and the listener. Its parts:

- **Pitch** — high or low. Lower, steady pitch sounds calm and confident.
- **Volume** — loud enough to be heard, never shouting; softer for private matters.
- **Pace (rate)** — slower for instructions, older people, anxious patients and numbers; slower still in a second language.
- **Tone** — warm, firm, urgent, sympathetic as the situation needs.
- **Emphasis** — stressing key words ("do **not** eat after midnight").

**Pause** — a short break in speech. It separates ideas, lets the listener think, highlights what comes next, and gives the speaker time to breathe. Pause after giving a number, a time or an instruction.

**Silence** — deliberately saying nothing. In therapeutic communication, a few seconds of silence after a patient shares bad news gives them time to feel and to continue. Silence must be attentive (with eye contact and open posture), not awkward or cold. Too long a silence in a formal talk, however, looks like forgetting.

## 2.7 R — Reading: medical vocabulary

Most medical words are built from Greek and Latin parts. Learn the parts and you can work out thousands of words.

```text
   PREFIX      +      ROOT (combining form)     +      SUFFIX
   brady-             card(i)/o                         -ia
   (slow)             (heart)                           (condition)
   → bradycardia = condition of slow heart rate
```

| Prefix | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a-, an- | without | anaemia, apnoea |
| brady- | slow | bradycardia |
| tachy- | fast | tachypnoea |
| dys- | difficult, painful | dysphagia, dyspnoea |
| hyper- | above, excess | hypertension |
| hypo- | below, deficient | hypoglycaemia |
| peri- | around | pericardium |
| endo- | within | endoscopy |
| post- / pre- | after / before | postoperative, prenatal |
| poly- | many | polyuria |

| Root | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cardi(o) | heart | cardiology |
| gastr(o) | stomach | gastritis |
| hepat(o) | liver | hepatomegaly |
| nephr(o), ren- | kidney | nephritis, renal |
| neur(o) | nerve | neurology |
| oste(o) | bone | osteoporosis |
| pulmon(o), pneum(o) | lung | pulmonary, pneumonia |
| derm(at)(o) | skin | dermatitis |
| haem(at)(o) | blood | haematuria |
| cyst(o) | bladder | cystitis |

| Suffix | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| -itis | inflammation | appendicitis |
| -ectomy | surgical removal | appendicectomy |
| -otomy | cutting into | tracheotomy |
| -ostomy | making an opening | colostomy |
| -algia | pain | neuralgia |
| -megaly | enlargement | splenomegaly |
| -scopy | looking inside with an instrument | bronchoscopy |
| -emia / -aemia | blood condition | septicaemia |
| -uria | urine condition | haematuria |
| -plasty | surgical repair | rhinoplasty |

Use a **medical dictionary or glossary**: check the meaning, the pronunciation (stress mark) and the plural. Some plurals are irregular: diagnosis → diagnoses, bacterium → bacteria, vertebra → vertebrae, ovum → ova, nucleus → nuclei, criterion → criteria.

## 2.8 Gr — Grammar: tenses

A **tense** shows the time of an action. English has three times (present, past, future), each with four aspects (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous) — 12 forms.

| Tense | Form | Nursing example | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Simple present | V1 / V1+s | The patient **complains** of headache. | Facts, habits, current state |
| Present continuous | is/am/are + V-ing | The drip **is running** well. | Action happening now |
| Present perfect | has/have + V3 | She **has vomited** twice since morning. | Past action linked to now; no exact time |
| Present perfect continuous | has/have been + V-ing | He **has been coughing** for three days. | Action that began in the past and continues |
| Simple past | V2 | The doctor **saw** the patient at 10 am. | Finished action at a stated time |
| Past continuous | was/were + V-ing | She **was sleeping** when I checked. | Action in progress at a past moment |
| Past perfect | had + V3 | The fever **had settled** before the doctor came. | The earlier of two past actions |
| Past perfect continuous | had been + V-ing | He **had been bleeding** for an hour before admission. | Duration up to a past moment |
| Simple future | will + V1 | I **will check** the dressing at 2 pm. | Decision, promise, prediction |
| Future continuous | will be + V-ing | We **will be shifting** her to the ward at noon. | Action in progress at a future time |
| Future perfect | will have + V3 | The drip **will have finished** by 6 pm. | Completed before a future time |
| Future perfect continuous | will have been + V-ing | By tomorrow he **will have been fasting** for 12 hours. | Duration up to a future time |

Rules nurses often break:

- Use the **simple past** with a stated past time: "I **gave** the injection at 8 am" — not "I have given the injection at 8 am".
- Nurses' notes are written in the **past tense** for what was observed and done ("Patient **ate** half of lunch"); the **present** for the present state ("Patient **is** drowsy but rousable").
- Third person singular takes **-s** in the simple present: "The patient **feels** dizzy" (not "feel").
- Irregular verbs: give–gave–given, take–took–taken, eat–ate–eaten, sleep–slept–slept, bleed–bled–bled, feel–felt–felt.

## 2.9 Linkers (connectives)

Linkers join ideas and show how they relate. They make writing and speech coherent.

| Purpose | Linkers | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Addition | and, also, in addition, moreover, furthermore | The wound is clean; moreover, there is no swelling. |
| Contrast | but, however, although, whereas, on the other hand | Although she slept, she still feels tired. |
| Cause | because, since, as, due to | He was restless because of pain. |
| Result | so, therefore, as a result, hence | His pulse rose; therefore, I informed the doctor. |
| Sequence | first, then, next, after that, finally | First wash your hands, then put on gloves. |
| Example | for example, for instance, such as | Use a soft diet, for example khichdi or porridge. |
| Condition | if, unless, provided that | Call me if the pain increases. |
| Summary | in short, to sum up, overall | In short, the patient is stable. |

Punctuation note: **however** and **therefore** in the middle of a sentence need a semicolon before and a comma after: "The patient was febrile; however, the pulse was normal."

## 2.10 W — Writing simple sentences and short paragraphs

A **simple sentence** has one subject and one main verb and expresses one complete idea: "The patient slept well."

Word order in English: **Subject – Verb – Object – Place – Time**: "The nurse (S) checked (V) the blood pressure (O) in the ward (P) at 6 am (T)."

Common faults:

- **Fragment** (incomplete sentence): "Because the patient was in pain." → "The patient could not sleep because he was in pain."
- **Run-on**: "The patient was in pain he could not sleep." → split with a full stop or a linker.
- **Subject–verb agreement**: "The list of patients **is** on the table" (the subject is "list").

A **paragraph** develops one idea: a **topic sentence** (main idea), **supporting sentences** (facts, examples) and a **concluding sentence**.

Model paragraph:

> Hand washing is the simplest way to prevent infection in hospital. Germs spread easily from one patient to another on the hands of staff. Washing with soap and water, or rubbing with an alcohol hand rub, removes most of these germs. Nurses should clean their hands before and after touching a patient, before a clean procedure and after contact with body fluids. If every member of the team follows this habit, infections in the ward fall sharply.

## 2.11 Paraphrasing and spelling

**Paraphrasing** means expressing someone's meaning in your own words without changing it. It is used to check understanding ("So you are saying the pain wakes you at night?"), to explain medical terms to patients, and to write assignments without copying.

- Original (doctor): "Keep the patient nil by mouth after midnight; surgery is planned for tomorrow."
- Paraphrase to the patient: "Please don't eat or drink anything after 12 tonight, because your operation is tomorrow."

Steps: read or listen until you understand → set the source aside → say it in your own words → compare to make sure the meaning is the same.

**Spelling** in records must be correct — a wrong spelling can change a medicine or a diagnosis. Words often misspelled: diarrhoea, haemorrhage, oesophagus, pneumonia, rhythm, temperature, separate, receive, occurred, accommodate, necessary, privilege, guarantee, unconscious. Indian records generally follow **British spelling**: haemoglobin (American: hemoglobin), oedema (edema), paediatric (pediatric), colour (color), centre (center), programme (program). Be consistent within one document.

## Remember

- LSRGW = listening, speaking, reading, grammar, writing.
- Hearing is passive; listening is active. Types: discriminative, comprehensive, critical, empathetic, appreciative, (selective, passive, active).
- 44 sounds in RP English: 24 consonants, 20 vowels (12 pure + 8 diphthongs). Schwa /ə/ is the commonest vowel.
- Word stress: nouns usually first syllable, verbs second; *-tion/-sion/-ic* words stress the syllable before.
- Content words are stressed; function words are weak. Falling intonation for statements and *wh*-questions, rising for yes/no questions.
- Voice modulation = pitch, volume, pace, tone, emphasis; pause separates ideas; silence gives space.
- Medical words = prefix + root + suffix.
- 12 tenses; nurses' notes use past tense for actions and present for current state.
- Linkers make writing coherent; paraphrase = same meaning, own words; use British spelling consistently.

# Unit 3: Attentive listening

This unit covers INC Unit III (5 hours). It teaches how to listen with full attention in different situations — announcements, descriptions, stories, instructions, discussions, demonstrations, lectures and presentations — and how to reproduce what was heard exactly when it matters.

## 3.1 What is attentive listening?

**Attentive (active) listening** is giving the speaker your full attention, understanding both the words and the feelings behind them, and showing through your responses that you have understood.

A nurse spends more of her working time listening than speaking, reading or writing. Patients often say the most important thing at the end of a conversation ("…and one more thing, doctor, I get chest pain when I climb stairs"). Only an attentive listener catches it.

Benefits of attentive listening:

- Accurate history and assessment — fewer missed symptoms.
- Fewer errors when receiving orders and handover.
- The patient feels respected and is more likely to trust and cooperate.
- Conflicts and complaints are calmed early.
- Better learning in class and in clinical teaching.

## 3.2 The listening process

```text
  RECEIVING  →  UNDERSTANDING  →  REMEMBERING  →  EVALUATING  →  RESPONDING
  (hear and      (attach meaning   (store key      (judge what    (feedback:
   attend)        to words, tone)   points)         is important)  nod, reply, act)
```

1. **Receiving** — hearing the sound and choosing to attend to it.
2. **Understanding** — working out the meaning of words, tone and non-verbal signs.
3. **Remembering** — keeping key facts long enough to use them (notes help).
4. **Evaluating** — separating fact from opinion, the important from the unimportant.
5. **Responding** — giving feedback: a nod, a question, a summary, or an action.

## 3.3 Barriers to attentive listening

| Barrier | Example | Remedy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Noise and interruptions | Phones, alarms, visitors | Choose a quieter place, close the curtain |
| Fatigue, hunger, worry | End of a night shift | Ask for a short repeat; write down key facts |
| Thinking ahead | Planning your reply instead of listening | Wait until the speaker finishes |
| Prejudging | "This patient always complains" | Listen fresh each time |
| Selective listening | Hearing only the part you expected | Listen for the whole message, then summarise |
| Language difficulty | Unfamiliar accent or word | Ask politely: "Could you say that again, please?" |
| Information overload | Long list of instructions | Ask the speaker to slow down; note as you listen |
| Distracting habits | Looking at a phone, fiddling with a pen | Put things down and face the speaker |

## 3.4 Skills of the active listener

### Non-verbal attending: SOLER

A simple guide to body language while listening:

- **S** — **S**it squarely facing the person (or at a slight angle).
- **O** — **O**pen posture: arms and legs uncrossed.
- **L** — **L**ean slightly towards the person.
- **E** — **E**ye contact: comfortable, not staring (adjust to culture).
- **R** — **R**elaxed manner.

### Verbal responses

| Technique | What it is | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Minimal encouragers | Short sounds or words that invite the speaker to continue | "Mm-hm", "I see", "Go on" |
| Open questions | Questions that cannot be answered yes/no | "How have you been sleeping?" |
| Closed questions | Yes/no or one-word answers, to check facts | "Did you take your morning tablet?" |
| Clarifying | Asking about something unclear | "When you say dizzy, do you mean the room spins?" |
| Paraphrasing | Restating the content in your own words | "So the pain began after lunch and is getting worse." |
| Reflecting feelings | Naming the emotion you notice | "You sound worried about going home alone." |
| Summarising | Pulling the main points together at the end | "Let me check I've got everything: …" |
| Silence | Giving time to think or feel | A pause after the patient becomes tearful |

Avoid **blocking responses**: false reassurance ("Don't worry, everything will be fine"), changing the subject, giving advice too quickly, judging ("You shouldn't feel like that"), and asking "why" in a way that sounds like blame.

## 3.5 Listening in different situations

### Announcements

Short, public and often repeated — at the hospital, railway station or over a public-address system. Listen for: **who** it concerns, **what** action is needed, **where** and **when**.

> "Attention please. All final-year students are to report to the Conference Hall on the second floor at 2 pm today for the infection control workshop."
> Key facts: final-year students · Conference Hall, 2nd floor · 2 pm today · infection control workshop.

### Descriptions

Describe a person, place, object or process. Listen for **features in order** — size, shape, colour, position, use. Example: a patient describing a wound or a relative describing a missing elderly patient.

### Narratives

Stories told in time order — a patient's history of illness or a colleague's account of an incident. Listen for **sequence words** (first, then, after that, finally) and **time expressions** (two days ago, last night). Draw a quick timeline in your notes.

### Instructions

Step-by-step directions. Listen for **action verbs**, **numbers**, **sequence words** and **warnings** ("do not", "never", "before"). Repeat the steps back before acting.

### Discussions

Several speakers giving views — a team meeting or a case conference. Listen for the **topic**, each speaker's **position**, the **reasons** given, points of **agreement**, and the **decision** reached.

### Demonstrations

A procedure shown and explained together — for example the clinical instructor demonstrating catheter care. Match each **spoken step** with the **action seen**; notice the rationale ("we clean from the meatus outwards because…"). Note the safety points.

## 3.6 Listening for different purposes

| Purpose | What you do | Example task |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Gist (overall meaning)** | Ignore details; get the main idea | "What is this news item about?" |
| **Specific information** | Listen only for the needed detail | "What time is the next dose?" "Which bed?" |
| **Detailed understanding** | Follow every point | Receiving handover or a telephone order |
| **Attitudes and opinions** | Notice tone, word choice and signal phrases | "I'm not very happy with…", "To be honest…", "I strongly feel…" |
| **Inference** | Work out what is meant but not said | "I don't want to be a burden" may hide fear of dependence |

Signals of **opinion**: I think, I feel, in my view, it seems, probably, I'm sure, I doubt. Signals of **fact**: dates, numbers, measurements, names, direct observations.

Listening tasks in class include multiple-choice, yes/no, true/false and fill-in-the-blank questions on announcements, news and short talks. Check your answers individually against the key, then listen again to find what you missed.

## 3.7 Reproducing verbatim

**Verbatim** means "word for word", exactly as spoken. Some information must never be summarised or changed:

- **Telephone or verbal orders** — written down at once and **read back** to the speaker word for word for confirmation. Hospitals limit verbal orders to emergencies and require the prescriber to sign them later; follow your hospital's policy.
- **Critical test results** reported by telephone — write them down and read them back.
- **A patient's own words** about symptoms, threats, refusals or complaints — recorded in quotation marks in the notes.
- **Names and numbers** — patient name, hospital number, bed number, times.
- **Statements in legal or incident situations** — what each person actually said.

Example of a verbatim entry in nurses' notes:

> 11.30 pm — Patient says, "I can't breathe properly when I lie flat." Propped up to 45°, respiratory rate 26/min. Doctor informed at 11.35 pm.

Read-back example on the telephone:

> Lab: "Bed 12, Mr Ravi Kumar, hospital number 4521, potassium is critical."
> Nurse: "Let me read that back: Bed 12, Mr Ravi Kumar, hospital number 4521, critical potassium result. I'm informing the doctor now. May I have your name, please?"

Tips: write while listening; use the speaker's exact words for anything you will quote; read back numbers digit by digit ("one-five, not fifty") because *fifteen* and *fifty*, *thirteen* and *thirty* are easily confused.

## 3.8 Listening to academic talks and lectures

Before the lecture:
- Read the topic in advance and revise the last class.
- Prepare your notebook with the date and title.

During the lecture:
- Listen for **signposting** language that shows the structure: "Today I'll cover three points…", "Firstly…", "Another important factor…", "To sum up…".
- Note **main ideas and key words**, not every word. Use abbreviations and symbols (↑ increase, ↓ decrease, → leads to, ∴ therefore, e.g., i.e., pt for patient).
- Mark points the teacher **repeats**, **writes on the board** or says are important — these are exam points.
- Note questions to ask at the end.

After the lecture: within a day, rewrite or tidy the notes, fill gaps from the textbook, and summarise in five lines.

### Note-taking formats

```text
CORNELL METHOD                         MIND MAP
+-----------+----------------------+         Barriers
| Cues /    | Notes taken during   |            |
| questions | the lecture          |  Process--COMMUNICATION--Types
|           |                      |            |
+-----------+----------------------+          7 Cs
| Summary (written after class)    |
+----------------------------------+
```

- **Outline method** — headings and indented sub-points.
- **Cornell method** — a narrow left column for key words and questions, a wide right column for notes, and a summary at the bottom.
- **Mind map** — the topic in the centre with branches for sub-topics; good for revision.

## 3.9 Listening to presentations

When a classmate or a speaker presents:

- Identify the **purpose** (inform, persuade, teach) and the **main message**.
- Follow the **structure**: introduction, main points, conclusion.
- Look at the **visuals** and connect them with what is said.
- Note **evidence** given for claims — figures, studies, examples.
- Give respectful **feedback**: one thing done well, one thing to improve, a question.

## 3.10 Attentive listening at the bedside — a model

> **Patient (Mrs Lakshmi, 62):** "I don't know… they said the operation went well, but I keep feeling something is wrong."
> **Nurse:** (sits beside the bed, eye contact) "You keep feeling something is wrong?" *(reflecting)*
> **Patient:** "My leg feels heavy and it's swollen since this morning."
> **Nurse:** "Tell me more about the swelling." *(open request)*
> **Patient:** "It's only the left leg, and it hurts in the calf when I move my foot."
> **Nurse:** "So since this morning your left leg is swollen and the calf hurts when you move your foot. Is that right?" *(paraphrasing and checking)*
> **Patient:** "Yes, exactly."
> **Nurse:** "Thank you for telling me. I'll check your leg now and inform the doctor straight away." *(responding with action)*

The nurse heard a worry, explored it, confirmed the facts and acted — a possible complication was reported early because she listened.

## Remember

- Hearing is physical; listening is active: receive → understand → remember → evaluate → respond.
- SOLER: Sit squarely, Open posture, Lean in, Eye contact, Relaxed.
- Active listening tools: encouragers, open questions, clarifying, paraphrasing, reflecting feelings, summarising, silence.
- Situations: announcements (who, what, where, when), descriptions, narratives (sequence), instructions (verbs, numbers, warnings), discussions, demonstrations.
- Purposes: gist, specific information, detail, attitude/opinion, inference.
- Verbatim = word for word: verbal orders and critical results are read back; patients' words go in quotation marks.
- Lectures: listen for signposts, note key words, use Cornell / outline / mind map, review within a day.

# Unit 4: Speaking — effective conversation, telephone talk, handover and presentations

This unit covers INC Unit IV (9 hours), the largest unit. It gives the phrases and patterns a nurse needs to speak well with patients, relatives, colleagues and doctors, face to face and on the telephone, and to present cases and give handover.

## 4.1 Conversation situations: formal, informal and neutral

| Situation | Features | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Formal** | Polite forms, full sentences, titles (Sir, Madam, Dr), no slang, set structure | Speaking to the Principal, a ward round, a viva, an interview |
| **Neutral** | Polite but relaxed; standard English; common in work | Talking to a patient, a colleague from another ward, a pharmacist |
| **Informal** | Short forms, first names, casual words | Chatting with a classmate or a close friend |

The same request at three levels:

- Formal: "Would you mind checking the drug chart for Bed 5, Sister?"
- Neutral: "Could you check the drug chart for Bed 5, please?"
- Informal: "Can you look at Bed 5's chart?"

**Register** is the choice of words and tone suited to the situation. Using an informal register with a senior or a patient's elderly relative can sound disrespectful; using a very formal register with a frightened child can sound cold.

## 4.2 Factors influencing the way we speak

1. **Setting** — place and time: an ICU at night needs a low voice; a classroom presentation needs a clear, carrying voice.
2. **Topic** — sensitive topics (death, sex, money, diagnosis) need gentle, private, careful language.
3. **Social relationship** — age, rank, familiarity: a senior consultant, a new patient, a peer.
4. **Attitude** — of the speaker and listener: respect, anger, anxiety, impatience change tone and words.
5. **Language** — shared language, vocabulary level, accent; use plain words with patients and technical words with professionals.

Other influences: culture (eye contact, touch, use of first names), the listener's health (hearing loss, pain, confusion), and the channel (face to face vs telephone).

## 4.3 Everyday speaking functions with useful phrases

### Greetings and introductions

- "Good morning, Mr Sharma. My name is Priya. I'm the nurse looking after you today."
- Introducing others: "Dr Mehta, this is Mrs Fernandes, the patient's daughter."
- Replying: "Pleased to meet you." / "Nice to meet you too."
- Leaving: "I'll be back at ten to check your drip. Press the call bell if you need me."

Always say your **name and role** and confirm the **patient's name** (two identifiers such as name and date of birth or hospital number before procedures).

### Requesting

- Polite: "Could you…, please?" "Would you mind…ing?" "I wonder if you could…"
- Example: "Would you mind turning onto your left side, please?"
- Replying: "Of course." / "Sure." / "I'm sorry, I can't right now, but…"

### Asking for and giving permission

- Asking: "May I check your blood pressure?" "Is it all right if I open the window?" "Do you mind if I sit here?"
- Giving: "Yes, of course." "Please go ahead."
- Refusing politely: "I'm afraid visitors are not allowed in the ICU now; visiting time is 4 to 6 pm."

Asking permission before touching or examining is part of respect and consent.

### Speaking personally and casual conversation

Small talk builds trust and gives clues about the patient's life: "How was your night?" "Is your family visiting today?" "What kind of work do you do?" Keep it brief, respectful and focused on the patient; avoid gossip, personal opinions on religion or politics, and sharing details of other patients.

### Asking for information

- Open: "Can you tell me about the pain?" "What happened before you fell?"
- Closed: "Do you have any allergies?" "Did you pass urine today?"
- Indirect (softer): "Could you tell me when you last ate?"

### Giving instructions and directions

Instructions — use the **imperative**, one step at a time, with sequence words:

> "First, wash your hands with soap. Then take the strip out of the box. Next, prick the side of your fingertip. After that, place the drop of blood on the strip. Finally, note the reading in your diary."

Directions — give landmarks and turns:

> "Go straight down this corridor, take the lift to the second floor, turn left, and the X-ray department is the second door on your right, opposite the pharmacy."

Check understanding: "Could you tell me how you'll do it at home?"

### Agreeing, disagreeing and giving opinions

| Function | Phrases |
| --- | --- |
| Giving an opinion | In my opinion…, I think…, I feel…, As far as I can see… |
| Agreeing | I agree., That's right., Exactly., I think so too. |
| Partly agreeing | That's true, but…, I agree up to a point, however… |
| Disagreeing politely | I'm not sure I agree., I see your point, but…, With respect, I think… |
| Asking for opinions | What do you think?, How do you feel about…? |

Disagreeing politely with a senior about patient safety is a duty, not rudeness: "Doctor, I'm concerned — the patient's BP is low; could you please review before we give the next dose?"

### Describing people, places, events and things

- **People**: age, build, height, clothes, distinguishing marks, behaviour. "An elderly man, about 70, thin, wearing a white kurta, walks with a stick."
- **Places**: location, size, layout, condition. "The isolation room is at the end of the ward; it has its own toilet and an anteroom."
- **Events**: what, when, where, who, how, result.
- **Things**: size, shape, colour, material, use. "A clear plastic bag with a tube and a clamp, used to collect urine."
- **Clinical descriptions**: a wound (site, size in cm, colour, discharge, smell), sputum (colour, amount, consistency), pain (site, type, severity, duration).

### Narrating, reporting and reaching conclusions

- **Narrating** — telling events in order with past tenses and time linkers: "At 2 am the patient woke up confused. He tried to climb out of bed. I raised the side rails and stayed with him, and then I informed the duty doctor."
- **Reporting** — passing on what others said (reported speech): "The patient said that he had not slept." "The doctor asked me to recheck the sugar at 6."
- **Reaching conclusions** — "From these readings, it seems that…", "So we can conclude that…", "Overall…".

Reported speech changes: present → past ("I am tired" → he said he **was** tired); *will* → *would*; *today* → *that day*; *here* → *there*.

### Evaluating and comparing

- Comparatives and superlatives: "Her pain is **less** today **than** yesterday." "This dressing is **more comfortable than** the old one." "This is **the best** position for her breathing."
- Weighing options: "On one hand… on the other hand…", "The advantage of… is…, but the drawback is…"

### Complaints and suggestions

**Receiving a complaint** (from a patient or relative) — five steps:

1. **Listen** without interrupting.
2. **Empathise**: "I understand how frustrating it is to wait so long."
3. **Apologise** for the experience (without blaming others): "I'm sorry this happened."
4. **Resolve** or explain what you will do: "I'll find out about the report and come back to you within half an hour."
5. **Follow up** and inform the in-charge if needed.

**Making a complaint** (for example about equipment) — be specific and calm: "The suction machine in Bed 3 isn't working; this is the second time this week. Could it be repaired today?"

**Suggestions** — "Why don't we…?", "How about…?", "It might help if…", "Shall we…?", "I suggest that…"

## 4.4 Telephone conversations

Telephone talk has no face or gestures, so voice and clarity matter more.

**Making a call**

1. Plan what you will say; keep the chart and a pen ready.
2. Greet and identify yourself and your area: "Good evening, this is Staff Nurse Anu from Medical Ward 3."
3. Check you have the right person: "Am I speaking to Dr Rao?"
4. State the purpose briefly (use SBAR for a clinical call — see 4.6).
5. Note the reply and **read back** any order or result.
6. Close politely: "Thank you, doctor. I'll do that now."
7. Document the call: time, person, message, response.

**Receiving a call**

- Answer promptly: "Medical Ward 3, Staff Nurse Anu speaking. How can I help you?"
- Take messages with: date and time, caller's name and number, message, action needed, your name.
- Never give confidential patient information to an unidentified caller; follow hospital policy.

**Clear telephone speech**: speak slowly; spell names using a phonetic alphabet ("R for Romeo, A for Alpha…"); say numbers digit by digit; avoid eating or side conversations; hold the receiver close.

Model message slip:

```text
Telephone message
Date/time: 12 March, 3.15 pm
For: Ward Sister, Surgical Ward
From: Mr Iqbal, Blood Bank, ext. 245
Message: Two units for Bed 18 (Mrs Kavita) are ready for collection.
Action: Send a staff member with the requisition slip.
Taken by: N. Joseph
```

## 4.5 Talking to patients, attenders and other professionals

**To patients and attenders** — use plain language, short sentences, no jargon; explain before acting; check understanding by teach-back; respect privacy; keep promises about time.

| Jargon | Plain words |
| --- | --- |
| NPO / nil by mouth | Nothing to eat or drink |
| Ambulate | Walk |
| Void | Pass urine |
| Hypertension | High blood pressure |
| Intravenous | Into a vein |

**To other professionals** — be brief, factual, organised, and use correct medical terms and units.

## 4.6 Handoff (handover) and SBAR

**Handover (handoff)** is the transfer of responsibility and information about a patient from one nurse or team to another at shift change, transfer between units, or for a procedure. Errors at handover are a major cause of missed care, so a **standard structure** is used.

### SBAR

| Letter | Meaning | What to say |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **S** | Situation | Who you are, which patient, what the problem is now |
| **B** | Background | Diagnosis, date of admission, relevant history, treatment so far |
| **A** | Assessment | Current findings: vital signs, observations, your judgement of the problem |
| **R** | Recommendation (Request) | What needs to be done, by whom, by when; what you are asking for |

Some hospitals use **ISBAR** (adding **I**dentify yourself and the patient first).

**Model SBAR call to a doctor**

> **S:** "Dr Rao, this is Staff Nurse Anu from Medical Ward 3. I'm calling about Mr Prakash Singh, Bed 9. His breathing has become fast in the last hour."
> **B:** "He is 58, admitted two days ago with pneumonia, on intravenous antibiotics and oxygen by nasal prongs."
> **A:** "His respiratory rate is 30 per minute, oxygen saturation has dropped to 89% on oxygen, pulse 118, temperature 38.6 °C, BP 110/70. He is anxious and using his neck muscles to breathe. I think his breathing is getting worse."
> **R:** "Could you please come and see him now? Should I increase the oxygen or prepare anything before you arrive?"
> (Doctor gives instructions; the nurse **reads them back**.)

**Model bedside shift handover (morning to afternoon)**

> "This is Mrs Radha Iyer, 45, Bed 4, second day after an abdominal hysterectomy. She has no known allergies. Overnight and this morning her vital signs were stable — last at 12 noon: temperature 37.2 °C, pulse 84, BP 120/80, respirations 18, pain score 3 out of 10 after her pain relief at 10 am. The wound dressing is dry and intact. She passed urine after the catheter was removed at 8 am — 300 ml at 11 am. She has started oral fluids and tolerated a light breakfast. She walked to the bathroom with help. Outstanding: blood test report for haemoglobin is awaited; next pain relief due at 4 pm if needed; she is anxious about going home and would like to talk to the dietitian. Any questions?"

Good handover is: at the bedside where possible (the patient can join), structured, up to date, focused on **changes, risks and pending tasks**, confidential, and ends with a chance to ask questions.

## 4.7 Reporting in doctors' and nurses' rounds

On rounds, the nurse reports briefly for each patient:

1. Name, bed, diagnosis, day of stay or day after surgery.
2. Overnight events and current condition (vital signs, intake–output, pain, sleep, wound).
3. Investigations done and results received.
4. Problems and concerns of the patient and nurse.
5. Questions for the doctor (clarify orders, discharge plans).

Speak clearly, use the chart, and note new orders immediately; confirm any order you are unsure about before the team leaves.

## 4.8 Presenting a situation in emergency and routine

**Emergency** — short, loud enough, facts first, clear request:

> "Emergency in Bed 7! Patient unresponsive, not breathing normally. Starting compressions — call the resuscitation team and bring the crash cart."

Use closed-loop communication: the leader gives a named instruction ("Ritu, bring the defibrillator"), the person repeats it ("Bringing the defibrillator") and confirms when done.

**Routine** — fuller, calmer, structured (SBAR or a ward-round report), with time for questions.

## 4.9 Case presentation

A **case presentation** is a structured oral report about one patient, given to teachers and peers.

Outline:

1. **Introduction** — patient's initials (keep identity private), age, sex, ward, date of admission, diagnosis.
2. **Chief complaints** with duration.
3. **History** — present illness, past, family, personal and social history.
4. **Physical examination** findings (head to toe, positive findings first).
5. **Investigations** and their results.
6. **Medical/surgical management** — the treatment plan (no need to recite every dose).
7. **Nursing assessment, nursing diagnoses, care plan** and evaluation.
8. **Health education** given and discharge plan.
9. **Summary** and questions.

Language tips: use past tense for history ("He was admitted on…"), present for current state ("He is now afebrile"); use signposts ("Moving on to the investigations…"); speak to the audience, not to your notes.

## 4.10 Delivering presentations

**Preparation**

- Know your **purpose** and **audience** (classmates, patients, a community group).
- Collect content; choose **3–5 main points**.
- Structure: **introduction** (greet, topic, why it matters, outline) → **body** (main points with examples) → **conclusion** (summary, key message, thank you, questions).
- Visuals: simple slides or charts — few words per slide, large font, one idea each; pictures and models help health talks.
- Rehearse aloud and time yourself.

**Delivery**

- Stand straight, smile, make eye contact around the room.
- Speak slowly and clearly, vary pitch and pause after key points.
- Use gestures naturally; avoid reading slides word for word.
- Handle questions: listen fully, repeat the question, answer briefly; if you don't know: "That's a good question; I'll find out and let you know."

**Useful signposting phrases**: "Good morning, everyone. Today I'm going to talk about…", "I've divided my talk into three parts…", "Let's start with…", "Moving on to…", "This brings me to my last point…", "To sum up…", "Thank you for listening. Are there any questions?"

## 4.11 Face-to-face oral communication — model nurse–patient conversation

> **Nurse:** "Good morning, Mr Das. I'm Meena, your nurse today. Could you tell me your full name and date of birth, please?"
> **Patient:** "Arun Das, fifth June, 1967."
> **Nurse:** "Thank you. The doctor has asked for a blood sample this morning. It's to check your sugar and kidney function. May I take it now?"
> **Patient:** "Will it hurt?"
> **Nurse:** "You'll feel a small prick, like an ant bite, for a second. I'll be quick and gentle."
> **Patient:** "All right."
> **Nurse:** (after the procedure) "All done. Please keep pressing the cotton for two minutes. Is there anything else I can do for you?"
> **Patient:** "No, thank you."
> **Nurse:** "Your breakfast will come at eight. I'll be back at nine to check on you."

The nurse introduced herself, identified the patient, explained the purpose and sensation, asked permission, reassured honestly, gave after-care instructions and told the patient when she would return.

## Remember

- Situations: formal, neutral, informal — choose the right register.
- Factors: setting, topic, social relationship, attitude, language.
- Functions: greet/introduce, request, permission, ask/give information, instruct/direct, agree/disagree, describe, narrate/report, evaluate/compare, complain/suggest.
- Telephone: identify self and area, state purpose, read back, note and document; spell names and say numbers digit by digit.
- Handover and calls to doctors: **SBAR** — Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation (ISBAR adds Identify).
- Rounds: name, diagnosis, events, findings, results, concerns, questions.
- Case presentation: identification → complaints → history → examination → investigations → management → nursing care → education → summary.
- Presentation: introduction, 3–5 points, conclusion; signposts, eye contact, pace, pauses.

# Unit 5: Reading — strategies, medical vocabulary, abbreviations, visuals, reports and remedial grammar

This unit covers INC Unit V (5 hours). It teaches how to read quickly and accurately — notes, messages, articles, charts, patient documents, doctors' prescriptions of care and reports — and revises the grammar points that most often cause errors.

## 5.1 Why reading accuracy matters

A nurse reads all day: case sheets, orders, medicine labels, lab reports, previous notes, policies and books. Misreading one letter or digit can lead to a wrong patient, wrong drug, wrong dose or wrong time. The rule is simple: **if you cannot read it clearly or do not understand it, ask — never guess.**

## 5.2 Reading strategies

| Strategy | What you do | When to use it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Skimming** | Read quickly for the main idea: title, headings, first and last lines of paragraphs, bold words | Deciding if an article is useful; getting the gist of a circular |
| **Scanning** | Run your eyes over the text looking for one specific item — a name, number, date, word | Finding a patient's allergy, a result, a phone extension |
| **Intensive reading** | Read slowly and carefully, every word, checking meaning | Orders, consent forms, procedures, exam questions |
| **Extensive reading** | Read longer texts for general understanding and pleasure | Novels, magazines, news — builds vocabulary and speed |
| **Critical reading** | Question the text: who wrote it, evidence, bias, fact or opinion | Health news, advertisements, research articles |

### The SQ3R method for study reading

1. **Survey** — look over headings, pictures, summaries.
2. **Question** — turn headings into questions ("What are the barriers to communication?").
3. **Read** — read actively to answer the questions.
4. **Recite** — say or write the answers without looking.
5. **Review** — go over the whole chapter again later.

### Guessing meaning from context

When you meet an unknown word, look at the words around it before reaching for a dictionary.

> "The patient was **lethargic**; she slept most of the day and responded slowly when spoken to."
> The sentence explains the word: lethargic = very drowsy and slow.

Clues: definitions ("that is", "which means"), examples ("such as"), contrast ("but", "unlike"), and word parts (prefix, root, suffix — Unit 2).

## 5.3 Reading notes and messages

Notes and messages are short and often abbreviated. Read for: **who** it is from and for, **what** is needed, **when** (deadline), and **any action** for you.

> *Note left at the nurses' station:* "Sr. Mary — Bed 14 relatives want to meet the doctor re: discharge. Dr. on OT till 2. Pls inform after 2 pm. — Ravi (8 am shift)"
> Meaning: Bed 14's family wants to talk to the doctor about discharge; the doctor is in the operation theatre until 2 pm; tell the doctor after 2 pm.

## 5.4 Reading articles and news items

- Read the **headline** and **first paragraph** — news puts the most important facts first (the inverted pyramid).
- Find the **5 Ws and 1 H**: who, what, where, when, why, how.
- Separate **facts** (numbers, dates, named sources) from **opinions** (adjectives, "experts feel", "it is believed").
- Check the **source** and **date** — health information changes; prefer official health department and journal sources over forwarded messages.
- Summarise in two or three sentences of your own.

## 5.5 Vocabulary for everyday activities and medical vocabulary

Words for daily care that patients and nurses use:

| Activity | Useful words |
| --- | --- |
| Hygiene | bed bath, sponge bath, mouth care, oral hygiene, shampoo, perineal care, nail care |
| Elimination | bedpan, urinal, commode, pass urine (void), motion/stool, constipation, incontinence |
| Mobility | turn, reposition, sit up, dangle legs, walk (ambulate), wheelchair, walking frame |
| Nutrition | diet, feed, appetite, swallow, sips, fluids, nasogastric tube |
| Comfort | pillow, backrest, side rails, call bell, blanket, fan |

Medical word building (prefix + root + suffix) is in Unit 2. Practise with matching exercises: match *nephrectomy* → removal of a kidney, *gastroscopy* → looking into the stomach, *dyspnoea* → difficult breathing.

## 5.6 Abbreviations

Hospitals keep an **approved abbreviation list**; use only those. Common ones:

| Abbreviation | Meaning | Abbreviation | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| BP | blood pressure | I/O | intake and output |
| TPR | temperature, pulse, respiration | NBM / NPO | nil by mouth |
| SpO2 | oxygen saturation by pulse oximeter | Stat | immediately |
| IV / IM / SC | intravenous / intramuscular / subcutaneous | PRN / SOS | when required |
| PO | by mouth | HS | at bedtime |
| BD / TDS / QID | twice / three times / four times a day | OD | once a day (but also "right eye" — ambiguous) |
| CBC | complete blood count | ECG | electrocardiogram |
| Hb | haemoglobin | ICU / OPD / OT | intensive care unit / outpatient department / operation theatre |
| c/o | complains of | h/o | history of |
| Dx / Rx / Tx | diagnosis / prescription, treatment / treatment | k/c/o | known case of |

**Dangerous abbreviations** — many hospitals forbid these because they are easily misread:

- "U" for units (can look like 0 or 4) — write "units".
- "IU" (can look like IV or 10) — write "international units".
- "QD" and "QOD" (daily and every other day are confused) — write "daily", "every other day".
- A trailing zero ("5.0" can be read as 50) — write "5".
- A missing leading zero (".5" can be read as 5) — write "0.5".
- Abbreviated drug names (two drugs may share the same letters) — write the full name.

If an abbreviation in an order has two possible meanings, **clarify with the prescriber before acting**.

## 5.7 Understanding visuals: graphs, tables, figures and flow sheets

Steps for reading any visual:

1. Read the **title** — what does it show?
2. Read the **labels and units** on each axis or column (°C, beats/min, ml, hours).
3. Note the **time scale** (hourly, 4-hourly, daily).
4. Look for the **trend**: rising, falling, steady, fluctuating.
5. Note **highest and lowest** values and anything **outside the normal range**.
6. Say in one or two sentences what it means and what action is needed.

```text
TEMPERATURE CHART (Bed 11)        °C
  39 |            *
  38 |       *         *
  37 | *  *                 *   *
     +-----------------------------
       6am 10am 2pm 6pm 10pm 2am 6am
Reading: temperature rose from 37 °C to a peak of 39 °C at 2 pm,
then fell back to 37 °C by 10 pm and stayed there overnight.
```

**Tables** — read across rows and down columns; check the row and column headings meet at the right cell.

**Flow sheets** — sheets on which repeated observations are entered at set times (vital-sign chart, intake–output chart, diabetic chart, neurological observation chart, fluid balance). Read the latest entry, then compare with earlier entries for change.

**Figures and diagrams** — read the caption and labels; connect each part to the text.

**Notes on instructions** — equipment labels and package inserts: read warnings, storage conditions, expiry date and steps in order.

## 5.8 Reading the patient document

The **case sheet / patient record** usually contains: identification data (name, age, sex, hospital number, ward, bed), admission notes and history, doctor's progress notes, **orders**, medicine administration record, nursing notes, vital-sign and intake–output charts, investigation reports, consent forms, and discharge summary.

When reading, check:

- **Right patient** — name and hospital number on every page.
- **Allergies** — usually flagged on the front.
- **Latest entries** — date and time order.
- **Legibility and signatures** — an unsigned or unclear order is clarified before acting.

## 5.9 Reading the doctor's prescription of care

A complete medicine order contains:

1. Patient's full name and identification.
2. Date and time of the order.
3. Name of the medicine (generic name preferred), written clearly.
4. Dose and units.
5. Route.
6. Frequency or exact times.
7. Duration or stop date (or "until review").
8. Special instructions (before food, after food, with water).
9. Prescriber's name and signature.

Other orders: diet ("soft diet", "diabetic diet"), activity ("bed rest", "ambulate"), position, investigations, observations ("hourly BP"), wound care.

The nurse checks the order against the **rights of medication administration** (right patient, drug, dose, route, time, and right documentation) — studied in detail in Nursing Foundations and Pharmacology. From an English point of view: read every word, check every abbreviation, and ask when in doubt.

## 5.10 Reading reports and interpreting them

**Laboratory report** — read: patient identifiers, test name, the patient's result, units, **reference (normal) range** column, and flags (H for high, L for low, often in bold or a different colour). Compare with the previous result to see the trend. Critical results are reported to the doctor at once.

**Radiology or other reports** — have two parts: **findings** (what was seen) and **impression / conclusion** (what it means). Read the impression first, then the findings.

**Incident or departmental reports** — find the event, time, people involved, action taken and recommendations.

Interpretation means not just reading the words but saying what they mean for the patient: "The haemoglobin is lower than the reference range and lower than last week's report — the doctor should be informed."

## 5.11 Idioms and phrases

Idioms are expressions whose meaning is not the sum of their words. Use them sparingly in speech; avoid them in records and with patients who may not understand them.

| Idiom / phrase | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| under the weather | slightly unwell | He's feeling under the weather today. |
| on the mend | recovering | The wound is on the mend. |
| back on one's feet | recovered | She'll be back on her feet in a week. |
| a bitter pill to swallow | an unpleasant fact to accept | Losing his job was a bitter pill to swallow. |
| in a nutshell | in brief | In a nutshell, the patient is stable. |
| keep an eye on | watch carefully | Keep an eye on his drip. |
| touch and go | uncertain, risky | It was touch and go during the night. |
| on duty / off duty | working / not working | I'm on night duty this week. |
| at the eleventh hour | at the last moment | The surgery was postponed at the eleventh hour. |
| break the ice | start a friendly conversation | Small talk helps break the ice with new patients. |
| hit the nail on the head | say exactly the right thing | Your answer hit the nail on the head. |
| burn the midnight oil | work late at night | Students burn the midnight oil before exams. |

## 5.12 Vocabulary for presentations

- Opening: "I'd like to talk about…", "The aim of my talk is…"
- Structuring: "firstly", "secondly", "moving on to", "let's now look at"
- Referring to visuals: "As you can see in this chart…", "This graph shows…", "The figures here indicate…"
- Describing trends: rise, increase, go up, peak; fall, decrease, drop, decline; remain steady, level off, fluctuate; sharply, gradually, slightly.
- Concluding: "To sum up…", "The key message is…", "Thank you for your attention."

## 5.13 Remedial grammar and spotting errors

### Articles

- **a** before a consonant **sound**, **an** before a vowel **sound**: a patient, a university (/j/ sound), an injection, an hour (silent h), an MRI ("em").
- **the** for something specific or already mentioned: "I gave her a tablet. **The** tablet was for pain."
- No article with general plural or uncountable nouns: "Nurses work hard." "Water is essential."

### Prepositions

| Correct | Common error |
| --- | --- |
| suffering **from** fever | suffering with fever |
| admitted **to** hospital **on** Monday **at** 6 pm | admitted in hospital at Monday |
| allergic **to** penicillin | allergic from penicillin |
| discuss the plan | discuss **about** the plan |
| cope **with** stress | cope up with stress |
| reply **to** the letter | reply the letter |
| comply **with** the rules | comply to the rules |

### Subject–verb agreement

- "Each of the patients **has** a call bell." (each = singular)
- "The team **is** ready." / "Neither the nurse nor the doctors **were** informed." (verb agrees with the nearer subject)
- "Mathematics / news **is**…"; "Scissors **are**…".

### Common Indian English usages to avoid in formal writing

| Avoid | Use |
| --- | --- |
| revert back | reply / reply to |
| do the needful | please take the necessary action (say what) |
| prepone | bring forward |
| return back | return |
| I am having fever | I have a fever |
| Myself Anu | I am Anu / My name is Anu |
| one of my friend | one of my friends |
| He is knowing | He knows |
| cousin brother | cousin |

### Spotting errors — practice with answers

1. "The patient have been vomiting since morning." → **has** been vomiting.
2. "She is suffering with diabetes since five years." → has been suffering **from** diabetes **for** five years.
3. "I have given the injection yesterday." → I **gave** the injection yesterday.
4. "Please discuss about the plan with the family." → discuss the plan.
5. "He is an unique case." → **a** unique case (/j/ sound).
6. "Each patients need a name band." → Each **patient needs**.
7. "The datas shows improvement." → The **data show** improvement.

## Remember

- Never guess an unclear order or abbreviation — ask.
- Skim for the main idea, scan for a detail, read intensively for orders and forms; SQ3R for study.
- Guess word meaning from context and word parts.
- Use only approved abbreviations; avoid U, IU, QD, QOD, trailing zeros and missing leading zeros.
- Visuals: title → labels and units → time scale → trend → highs/lows → meaning.
- A complete medicine order: patient, date/time, drug, dose, route, frequency, duration, instructions, signature.
- Lab report: result, units, reference range, flags, trend.
- Remedial grammar: articles by sound, correct prepositions, subject–verb agreement, no "discuss about", "cope up", "revert back".

# Unit 6: Writing skills — patient history, notes, letters, reports, journals, abstracts and CV

This unit covers INC Unit VI (5 hours). It gives the formats and model examples for the writing a nurse does in practice and as a student. Writing is assessed for **task fulfilment, coherence and cohesion, appropriate vocabulary and correct grammar** — keep these four in mind for every answer.

## 6.1 Qualities of good writing

| Quality | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Task fulfilment | Answers exactly what was asked, in the right format and length |
| Coherence | Ideas in a logical order; each paragraph has one main idea |
| Cohesion | Sentences linked with linkers (however, therefore, then) and pronouns that refer back clearly |
| Appropriate vocabulary | Words suited to the reader: technical for professionals, plain for patients |
| Correct grammar and spelling | Tenses, agreement, punctuation, spelling (Units 2 and 5) |

The writing process: **plan** (purpose, reader, points) → **draft** → **revise** (content, order) → **edit** (grammar, spelling) → **final copy**.

## 6.2 Principles of documentation

Nursing records are **legal documents**. In a dispute, the record is the evidence of care: "if it was not written, it was not done."

- **Factual** — record what you see, hear, measure and do; not guesses or labels ("patient is rude" ✗; "patient shouted, 'Leave me alone'" ✓).
- **Accurate** — exact measurements, times and spelling; use approved abbreviations only.
- **Complete** — all care, observations, responses and communication with others.
- **Current (timely)** — write as soon as possible after the event; never before doing it.
- **Organised** — in time order, with date and time for every entry.
- **Legible and permanent** — clear handwriting in ink (or the hospital's electronic system).
- **Signed** — name, designation and signature.
- **Confidential** — records are shared only with those involved in care.

Errors: draw a **single line** through the mistake so it is still readable, write "error" (or the hospital's term), initial and date it, then write the correct entry. Never use correction fluid, never overwrite, never tear out pages, and never leave blank lines (draw a line through empty space).

## 6.3 Writing patient history

A **patient history** is a written account of the patient's health information collected by interview.

Format:

```text
IDENTIFICATION DATA: Name, age, sex, hospital no., ward/bed, date of admission,
                     address, religion, education, occupation, informant
CHIEF COMPLAINTS (with duration): in the patient's words where possible
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: onset, duration, course, associated symptoms,
                     treatment taken
PAST HISTORY: illnesses, surgeries, admissions, allergies, immunisation
FAMILY HISTORY: similar illness, hereditary conditions
PERSONAL HISTORY: diet, sleep, bowel and bladder habits, habits (tobacco, alcohol)
SOCIO-ECONOMIC HISTORY: family type, income, housing, support
```

Model (history of present illness):

> Mrs S, 54 years, was admitted on 10 March with complaints of "burning while passing urine for four days" and fever with chills for two days. She also reports passing urine frequently, about every hour. She took paracetamol from a local shop with temporary relief. There is no history of blood in urine or loin pain. She is a known case of diabetes for eight years, on tablets.

Write history in the **past tense**, report the patient's words in quotation marks, and keep opinions out.

## 6.4 Nurses' notes and written handover

**Nurses' notes** record the patient's condition, the care given and the response. Common formats:

| Format | Parts |
| --- | --- |
| Narrative | Time-ordered paragraphs of observations and care |
| SOAP / SOAPIE | Subjective (what the patient says), Objective (what you observe/measure), Assessment (your judgement), Plan, Intervention, Evaluation |
| DAR (focus charting) | Data, Action, Response — under a focus heading such as "Pain" |

Model narrative entry:

> **14/03, 2.00 pm** — Patient complains of pain at the operation site, 6/10 on the pain scale, "like a pulling feeling." Grimacing on moving. T 37.4 °C, P 96/min, R 20/min, BP 130/84 mmHg. Dressing dry and intact. Pain relief given as ordered (see medicine chart). Positioned on the left side with a pillow supporting the abdomen.
> **2.45 pm** — Pain now 2/10; patient resting comfortably. — *Signature, N. Kaur, Staff Nurse*

Model SOAPIE entry (focus: breathing):

> **S:** "I feel short of breath when I walk to the toilet."
> **O:** RR 26/min, SpO2 92% on room air, using accessory muscles after walking 10 metres.
> **A:** Breathlessness on exertion.
> **P:** Reduce exertion, oxygen as ordered, inform doctor.
> **I:** Placed in high Fowler's position, oxygen started as ordered, doctor informed at 10.20 am, commode placed at bedside.
> **E:** At 10.45 am RR 20/min, SpO2 96%, patient says breathing is easier.

**Written handover note** (shift report) — for each patient: name, age, bed, diagnosis, day of stay; current condition and vital signs; care given; changes and incidents; investigations pending; medicines or procedures due; risks (falls, pressure injury, infection); family concerns. Use SBAR headings for clarity (Unit 4).

## 6.5 Note taking and summarising

**Note taking** — writing down key points from a lecture, book or meeting for later use. Use headings, short phrases, abbreviations, numbering and symbols; leave space; use the Cornell or mind-map format (Unit 3).

**Summarising** — reducing a text to its main ideas in your own words, usually one-third or less of the original.

Steps:

1. Read the whole text to understand it.
2. Underline the main idea of each paragraph.
3. Leave out examples, repetition and minor details.
4. Write the main ideas in your own words, linked logically.
5. Check that the meaning is unchanged and nothing important is missing.
6. Give a title.

Model — original (about 110 words):

> Falls are a common and serious problem among elderly patients in hospital. A fall may cause fractures, head injuries, fear of walking and a longer stay. Many factors increase the risk: weakness, dizziness, poor eyesight, confusion, the need to pass urine at night, wet floors, poor lighting and unfamiliar surroundings. Some medicines that cause drowsiness also raise the risk. Nurses can prevent most falls by assessing every patient's risk on admission, keeping the bed low with the brakes on, placing the call bell and personal items within reach, helping patients to the toilet, keeping floors dry and lights on at night, and teaching patients to rise slowly.

Summary (about 40 words):

> **Preventing falls in elderly patients.** Falls in hospital cause injury and longer stays. Weakness, confusion, poor vision, night-time toileting, drowsy medicines and unsafe surroundings increase risk. Nurses prevent falls by assessing risk, making the bedside safe, helping with toileting and teaching patients.

## 6.6 Anecdotal records

An **anecdotal record** is a brief, factual written description of a specific incident of a student's (or patient's) behaviour, written soon after it is observed, with the observer's comment kept separate. Teachers use it to assess students' clinical performance; nurses may use similar records for patient behaviour.

Features: one incident per record, objective description, date, time and place, separate interpretation, signed.

Model:

```text
ANECDOTAL RECORD
Student: Ms R. Thomas        Year: 1st B.Sc Nursing     Area: Female Medical Ward
Date/time: 18/03, 10.15 am   Observer: Clinical Instructor
Incident: While giving a bed bath to an elderly patient, the student closed the
curtains, explained each step, covered parts of the body not being washed, and
asked the patient if the water was warm enough. When the patient said she felt
cold, the student added a blanket at once.
Comment: Shows respect for privacy and dignity and responds to patient needs.
Recommendation: Continue; encourage her to share this practice with peers.
Signature of observer: ________   Signature of student: ________
```

## 6.7 Letter writing

### Formal letter format

```text
Sender's address
Date

Receiver's designation and address

Subject: (one line saying what the letter is about)

Salutation (Respected Sir/Madam, / Dear Sir/Madam,)

Body: paragraph 1 — purpose
      paragraph 2 — details
      paragraph 3 — request or action and thanks

Closing (Yours faithfully, / Yours sincerely,)
Signature
Name and designation
```

Use **"Yours faithfully"** when the salutation is "Dear Sir/Madam" (name not known); **"Yours sincerely"** when you address the person by name. Keep it short, polite and to the point.

**Model 1 — Leave application**

> To
> The Principal,
> College of Nursing, …
>
> 22 March 2026
>
> Subject: Application for leave for three days
>
> Respected Madam,
>
> I am a first-year B.Sc Nursing student. I request leave from 24 to 26 March 2026 to attend my sister's wedding in my home town.
>
> I will complete the missed classes and clinical assignments on my return.
>
> Kindly grant me leave for these three days.
>
> Thanking you,
> Yours faithfully,
> (Signature)
> Anjali Verma, Roll No. 12, 1st year B.Sc Nursing

**Model 2 — Letter to the Nursing Superintendent requesting equipment**

> To
> The Nursing Superintendent, District Hospital, …
>
> Subject: Request for replacement of two non-working suction machines in the Paediatric Ward
>
> Respected Madam,
>
> Two of the three suction machines in the Paediatric Ward have not been working since 15 March. The biomedical department has examined them and reported that they cannot be repaired.
>
> With an average of 25 children admitted, several of them with respiratory problems, one machine is not enough, especially at night and in emergencies.
>
> I request that two new suction machines be supplied as early as possible. The biomedical report is attached.
>
> Yours faithfully,
> (Signature)
> Ward In-charge, Paediatric Ward

Other letters students should practise: letter to a patient's family about a follow-up visit, a complaint about poor hostel facilities, a requisition to the store, a letter of thanks to a hospital for a field visit, and a job application with CV.

**Informal letter** (to a friend or family member): address and date, "Dear …", friendly paragraphs, "With love / Yours affectionately", first name. No subject line.

**E-mail** follows the formal letter in tone: clear subject line, greeting, short paragraphs, sign-off with name and designation, check before sending.

## 6.8 Diary and journal writing

A **diary** is a personal day-to-day record. A **reflective journal** is a written reflection on learning experiences — used in nursing education to link theory and practice and to grow professionally.

A common structure for reflection is **Gibbs' reflective cycle**:

1. **Description** — what happened?
2. **Feelings** — what were you thinking and feeling?
3. **Evaluation** — what was good and bad about the experience?
4. **Analysis** — what sense can you make of it? (link to theory)
5. **Conclusion** — what else could you have done?
6. **Action plan** — what will you do if it happens again?

Model reflective journal entry (short):

> **Date: 5 April.** Today I took the blood pressure of an elderly patient for the first time without help. My hands shook and I had to repeat it twice. I felt nervous because the patient's son was watching. Afterwards, the patient thanked me and said I was gentle. I realise I was worried about being judged rather than focusing on the technique. Explaining the procedure first, as we learned in class, would have relaxed both of us. Next time I will explain each step aloud and practise more on classmates during lab hours.

Write in the **first person** and **past tense** for events; be honest and keep patient identities confidential.

## 6.9 Report writing

A **report** is a formal, factual account of an event, activity or investigation, written for a specific reader, usually with headings.

General format:

```text
Title
To / From / Date
1. Introduction (purpose, background)
2. Details / Findings (what happened, in order)
3. Action taken
4. Conclusion / Recommendations
Signature, name, designation
```

**Model — Incident report (patient fall)**

> **Incident report**
> **Patient:** Mr K. Nair, 76 years, Bed 21, Male Medical Ward, Hosp. No. 30718
> **Date and time of incident:** 9 April, 3.10 am
> **Description:** At 3.10 am the patient was found sitting on the floor beside his bed. He said, "I wanted to go to the toilet and my legs gave way." The side rails were down; the call bell was on the bedside table out of his reach.
> **Assessment after the fall:** Conscious and oriented. Complained of pain in the right hip. No visible bleeding. T 36.8 °C, P 92/min, R 20/min, BP 140/90 mmHg.
> **Action taken:** Patient lifted back to bed with the help of two staff. Duty doctor informed at 3.15 am and examined him at 3.25 am; X-ray of the right hip ordered. Side rails raised, call bell placed within reach, urinal kept at bedside. Family informed at 7 am.
> **Recommendations:** Fall-risk assessment for all elderly patients on admission; night-time toileting rounds.
> **Reported by:** S. Pillai, Staff Nurse — 9 April, 4.00 am

Other reports: ward (shift) report, report of a health camp or field visit, report on a seminar, monthly census report. Use the **past tense**, the **passive voice** where the doer is not important ("The patient was shifted to ICU"), and objective language.

## 6.10 Paper writing skills

A **paper** (assignment, term paper or research article) presents information or findings on a topic in an organised, referenced way.

1. **Choose and narrow the topic** — "Hand hygiene compliance among nursing students" rather than "Infection".
2. **Search the literature** — textbooks, journals, official guidelines; note references as you read.
3. **Outline** — introduction, main sections, conclusion.
4. **Write the draft** in your own words — **paraphrase and cite**; copying without citing is **plagiarism**.
5. **Cite sources** in the text and list them in references in the style your college uses (for example Vancouver or APA).
6. **Revise** for logic and **edit** for language; read aloud; check figures and tables are numbered and titled.

Academic style: formal, objective, precise; avoid "I think", slang and contractions ("don't" → "do not"); define terms when first used; one idea per paragraph.

## 6.11 Abstract writing

An **abstract** is a short, complete summary of a paper (usually 150–300 words; follow the limit given) placed at the beginning so readers can decide whether to read the whole paper.

A **structured abstract** follows **IMRaD**:

- **Background / Introduction** — the problem and aim.
- **Methods** — design, setting, sample, tools.
- **Results** — the main findings with key figures.
- **Discussion / Conclusion** — what the results mean and recommendations.
- **Keywords** — 3–5 terms.

Model structured abstract (fictitious study for practice):

> **Background:** Hand hygiene prevents hospital infections, but students may not follow it consistently. This study aimed to assess hand hygiene practice among first-year nursing students.
> **Methods:** A descriptive study was conducted with 60 first-year students in a teaching hospital. Practice during clinical postings was observed with a checklist based on the five moments of hand hygiene.
> **Results:** Students cleaned their hands most often after body-fluid exposure and least often before touching a patient. Practice improved when hand-rub dispensers were placed at the bedside.
> **Conclusion:** Hand hygiene before patient contact needs reinforcement through teaching and reminders.
> **Keywords:** hand hygiene, nursing students, infection prevention

Write it **last**, in the past tense for methods and results, with no references or abbreviations that are not explained.

## 6.12 Resume / curriculum vitae

A **resume** is a short (1–2 page) summary of qualifications for a job; a **CV** is a fuller academic record. For a fresh nurse they look similar.

```text
NAME
Address | Phone | E-mail
CAREER OBJECTIVE: one or two lines about the role you want
EDUCATION: degree, college, university, year, grade (latest first)
REGISTRATION: State Nursing Council registration number (when obtained)
CLINICAL EXPERIENCE: areas of posting / work, duration
SKILLS: clinical skills, computer skills, languages known
TRAINING / CERTIFICATES: e.g. life-support courses, workshops
ACHIEVEMENTS AND ACTIVITIES: awards, positions, community work
REFERENCES: two referees with designation and contact (or "available on request")
DECLARATION, place, date, signature
```

Tips: latest information first; action words (assisted, managed, organised, conducted); no spelling errors; honest; send with a short covering letter.

## 6.13 Verbatim reproducing and presenting a situation in writing

- **Verbatim** writing quotes exactly what was said or written, in quotation marks — patients' statements, telephone orders (also read back), critical results. Do not "correct" the patient's grammar inside a quotation.
- **Presenting a situation** in writing (for example a change in a patient's condition) is best done with the SBAR headings, so the reader sees the problem, background, findings and request at once.

## Remember

- Writing is judged on task fulfilment, coherence and cohesion, vocabulary and grammar.
- Documentation: factual, accurate, complete, timely, organised, legible, signed, confidential; single-line corrections.
- History: identification → chief complaints → present, past, family, personal, socio-economic history.
- Nurses' notes: narrative, SOAPIE, DAR; record the patient's words in quotation marks.
- Summary = main ideas in your own words, about one-third length.
- Anecdotal record: one incident, objective, dated, with a separate comment.
- Formal letter: address, date, receiver, subject, salutation, body, "Yours faithfully/sincerely", signature.
- Reflective journal: Gibbs — description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, action plan.
- Report: title, introduction, details, action, recommendations, signature; past tense, objective.
- Abstract: IMRaD in 150–300 words; written last. CV: latest first, honest, error-free.
